title.p: The Shadow Files · Vol. I: Foundations

section.p: This book is an educational introduction to open-source intelligence — OSINT — written for beginners and for anyone who wants to understand how information about people and organisations can be found, verified, and protected using only what is already public.

Everything in these pages is taught inside a strict ethical and legal frame: open sources only, nothing that requires unauthorised access, and full respect for privacy and for the law. Laws differ from country to country — and more than one country's laws can apply to a single search. Know the rules where you are, and when you are not sure, get permission first.
section.subtitle: Everything here is invented
section.p: Every name, username, email address, phone number, photograph, and case study in this book is entirely fictional. Each one was created to teach a method — never to describe a real person. Any resemblance to a real individual, account, or event is pure coincidence.
section.subtitle: Why the examples are shown in full
section.p: So the lessons feel real, the examples use complete, ordinary-looking data instead of blanked-out symbols. Because every detail is invented, nothing here can touch a real person — and you still see exactly how a real trail looks and behaves.
section.subtitle: The rule that outranks every technique
section.p: Understanding how people become exposed exists here for one reason: to investigate responsibly, and to protect yourself and others better. Chapter 2 makes the ethical and legal boundaries concrete; for now, hold one line — use what you learn lawfully, ethically, and with care.
section.subtitle: If you came here to protect yourself
section.p: Some readers open this book not to investigate anyone, but because they are worried about being found — by a stranger, an ex, a harasser. You are welcome here, and this book is for you too. You do not have to read eight chapters first: skip to Appendix D, "Take it back" for a plain, prioritised checklist of how to shrink your own footprint, then come back to the start whenever you are ready. Understanding how exposure works is exactly what lets you shut it down.

cite.p: A professional is not the person who can find the most. It is the person who knows where to stop.

section.p: This book was written for people starting from zero.
You do not need to be a hacker. You do not need to write code. You do not need special software or a powerful computer. If you can use a search bar, you already have everything you need to begin.
section.subtitle: This is for you if you are
section.p: • Completely new and simply curious how investigators find things out.
• Someone who wants to protect yourself — to see what a stranger could learn about you, and shut those doors.
• A future analyst or investigator who wants a real, professional method from the very first page.
• A working professional — in HR, security, journalism, or law — who needs a structured, defensible way to check people and claims.
section.subtitle: What you will be able to do by the end
section.p: Take one small clue — a username, an email, a phone number — and, step by step, responsibly build a clear and honest picture around it. Not by guessing. By method.
That is the whole promise of this first volume: the foundations that everything else is built on.

epigraph.p: The series, this volume, and how each chapter is built.

section.p: The Shadow Files is a series of four volumes. Each one takes you one clear level higher, and each one assumes only what the last one taught.
• Volume 1 — Foundations. The mindset, the rules, and your first real skills. (This book.)
• Volume 2 — Cross-Platform Attribution. Following a person across social networks, messengers, photos, and leaks.
• Volume 3 — Hard Targets. Deleted accounts, geolocation, infrastructure, and the unusual tricks that surprise people.
• Volume 4 — The Professional. Corporate work, reports, counter-investigation, and turning skill into a craft.

A note on scope, so you know what you are holding: this volume is about finding and verifying people from the traces they leave. Hunting infrastructure — domains, servers, subdomains, exposed files, the recon a penetration tester lives on — is real OSINT too, but it is a different toolkit, and it waits for Volume 3. If you came for asset recon, you are early, not in the wrong place.

section.subtitle: How every chapter is built
section.p: The same simple rhythm, every time, so you always know where you are:
• The idea — in plain words, no jargon.
• The method — how a professional actually thinks and works, step by step.
• A worked case — a short, invented investigation you can follow move by move.
• An exercise — something safe and legal you do yourself.
• A recap — the three things to remember.
section.subtitle: One promise about tools
section.p: This series teaches method first, tools second. Websites and apps come and go — some named here may be gone by the time you read this, and new ones will have taken their place. That is fine. The thinking never changes. Learn the method, and any tool becomes just a faster way to do something you already understand.

epigraph.p: It always starts with one small thing.

section.p: A username someone chose years ago and forgot. A photo posted in a good mood. A phone number typed into the wrong box. A single line in an old profile.
None of it looks like much. That is exactly why it is so powerful.

People imagine that finding out about someone takes secret tools, or breaking in, or some dark corner of the internet. It doesn't. Almost everything that matters is sitting in the open, in plain sight, left there by ordinary people living ordinary lives. The work is not about breaking locks. It is about noticing — and knowing what to do with what you notice.
That is the craft this series will teach you. Not tricks. A way of seeing.

You will learn to take one small, forgotten thing and follow it — carefully, honestly — until it quietly tells you a story. You will also learn the other half, the half most people skip: how much you are giving away, and how to take it back.

I have spent years doing this work — in law enforcement, in private investigations, and teaching it to professionals around the world. And the most important thing I can tell you before we start is this: the power to see clearly comes with the duty to use it well. We will talk about that duty often, because it is what separates a professional from everyone else.
Everyone leaves a shadow. By the end of this book, you will know how to read one — and, just as importantly, when to look away.

cite.p: Every shadow has a name. Let's learn how to find it.

section.subtitle: Chapter One
section.p: Let's start with the honest version, no jargon.

OSINT means finding out about a person or a thing using only what's already out in the open. No hacking. No breaking in. No logging into anyone's account. Everything you'll ever do in this book uses doors that are already unlocked — public profiles, public posts, public records, public photos. You're not a burglar. You're someone who reads what everybody left lying on the table.

That's the first thing to unlearn: you don't need to be a "hacker." You need two things — the willingness to look, and a way to think. The looking is easy. This whole book is really about the thinking.
section.subtitle: The one idea everything is built on
section.p: Here it is, the entire craft in one line:

cite.p: Everyone leaves traces. You start from one trace, follow it to the next, and keep going until the pieces point to a real person.

section.p: We give those three moves names, and you'll hear them for the rest of the series:
• 1. Exposure — the trace a person left behind (a username, a photo, a phone number, an old post).
• 2. Pivot — using that trace to find the next one. One clue hands you another.
• 3. Attribution — when enough clues line up and point at a single, real identity.
Exposure → pivot → attribution. That's it. Every case in every book is just this loop, run again and again.

Picture a loose thread on a sweater. You don't attack the whole sweater. You find one thread and pull — gently — and it leads to the next stitch, and the next. OSINT is pulling threads. The skill is knowing which thread, and how hard to pull.
section.subtitle: How an investigator actually thinks
section.p: Four habits separate a professional from someone just typing a name into a search bar.
• Start from one point. Not "who is this person" — that's too big to answer. Instead: "I have this one username. What can it give me?" Small questions have answers.
• Every answer is a new question. Found an email? Good — now, where else does that email live? You are never finished; you just pivot to the next question.

• Similar is not the same. Two accounts using the nickname "shadowfox" are not automatically the same human. This is the mistake that ruins beginners. You don't conclude — you confirm, with a second and a third independent clue.

• Watch your own wishes. You will want the clue to point at your target — and that wanting is the danger. The moment you feel sure, deliberately hunt for the fact that would prove you wrong. That single habit will save you more grief than any tool.
• It's structured curiosity. Not magic, not luck. A calm, repeatable process anyone can learn.
section.subtitle: A tiny example, so you can see the loop

p.emphasis: Everything below is invented — a made-up person, to show the thinking, not the tools.

section.p: You're handed one thing: the username j.karas_88.
• Step 1 — Exposure. You check where that exact username exists across platforms. It turns up on a gaming forum and an old photo-sharing site.
• Step 2 — Pivot. The forum profile mentions a city, Riverton, and links a second nickname: jaykaras. A new thread to pull.
• Step 3 — Pivot again. That second nickname appears on a public profile that shows a first name, Jason, and a contact address: jaykaras88@mailbox.com.
• Step 4 — Confirm, don't assume. Same city on two sites. The same profile photo on both. The same odd way of writing ("cheers all!"). Three independent signals now point the same way.
• Step 5 — Attribution. You're no longer guessing. One username has become a named person — because each step earned the next.
Notice what did the work. No clever tool. The pivots did. Tools only speed up steps you already understand — which is exactly why this series teaches the method first.

The first time I did this for real, I started with a single username and a bad feeling. I did not expect much. An hour later I was looking at the whole shape of a person — where they worked, who they knew, the city they woke up in — built entirely from scraps they had left in the open, one small step at a time. Nobody handed me any of it; I had simply asked the right small questions in the right order. I have never forgotten that feeling. Not power, exactly — more like the quiet click of a lock you did not force, only understood.
section.subtitle: The one rule that never bends
section.p: Everything here stays on the public side of a single line: open sources only, nothing you'd need permission for. The next chapter draws that line in full — where it runs, why it holds, and why staying on the right side of it makes you more effective, not less.
section.subtitle: Your first exercise
section.p: Investigate the easiest target you'll ever have — yourself.
• Write down the oldest username you ever used (that gaming or forum handle from years ago).
• Search it, exactly, across a few platforms.
• See what still exists, what it links to, and — honestly — how far a stranger could pivot from it.
You'll learn two things at once: how the loop feels, and how exposed you already are.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • OSINT is building a picture from only public information — no hacking.
• The whole craft is one loop: exposure → pivot → attribution.
• Method beats tools. Start small, pivot, and confirm before you conclude.

p.emphasis: Next: the rules — where the line is, and why staying on the right side of it makes you more effective, not less.

epigraph.p: Law, ethics, and the lines you never cross

section.subtitle: Chapter Two
section.p: Start with the most reassuring thing I can tell you. Almost everything you will learn in this book is completely legal, completely open, and something you can do with a clear conscience. OSINT is built on looking at what people, companies, and governments have already made public. You are not breaking in anywhere. You are reading what is already on the shelf.

So this chapter is not here to scare you. It is here to hand you a compass. Once you understand a few simple ideas, you will feel where the line is, and you will not have to look it up every time. Here is the surprising part: the people who understand the rules best are also the boldest investigators. They move fast because they never worry that they crossed a line. Knowing where the wall is lets you run right up to it — so let me show you where it stands.
section.subtitle: The bright line — looking versus touching
section.p: There is one line that matters more than all the others. Picture it as a bright, glowing line painted on the floor. Everything you do in OSINT falls on the safe side of it or the wrong side of it, and the line itself is simple.

cite.p: Looking at what is already public is fine. Getting into what is locked is not.

section.p: That is the whole thing. In plainer words:

• On the safe side: reading a public profile, a company registration, a news article, a photo someone posted, a phone number listed in an open directory. All of this is out in the open. Anyone can see it. You are a member of the public looking at public things.
• On the wrong side: logging into someone else's account, guessing or using someone's password, sneaking past a login screen, getting into anything that was meant to be private and protected.

Think of a house on a street. You are allowed to walk down the street and look at the house. You can see the colour, the garden, the car in the driveway, the name on the mailbox. That is all public. You are not allowed to open the front door and walk in — even if you happen to know a key is under the mat. The moment you touch that door, you have crossed the line, no matter how easy it was.

In the computer world, the "front door" is anything with a password, a login, or a lock. If a step requires you to sign in as someone else or get around a security control, stop. That is the signal. That is the bright line, and you have reached it.

There are even laws with names attached to this idea. In the United States there is a law often called the CFAA — the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. You do not need to memorise it. You just need its one-sentence heart: using a password you found to log into an account that is not yours is "unauthorised access," and it is a crime. Reading that an account exists is fine. Opening it is not. Same house, same door.
section.subtitle: Public does not always mean fair game
section.p: Here is where beginners get tripped up.

"If it is public, I can do anything with it." That feels true. It is not. Something can be out in the open and still deserve respect: being allowed to see a thing is not the same as being allowed to collect it, store it forever, and use it for any purpose you like.

cite.p: Public gives you permission to look. It does not hand you permission to do anything you want.

section.p: An example makes this obvious. Imagine someone posts a photo in a small support group for people recovering from an illness. Technically you can find it. But that person shared it in a small, gentle corner of the internet, expecting a small, gentle audience. If you rip it out of that corner and paste it into a report about them, you have done something that is legal to see but wrong to use that way. You broke the promise the setting made to them.

Professionals have a rule for this, and it is beautiful in its simplicity: respect the original context. Ask yourself, "Why did this person share this, and where?" The words may be public either way. The spirit is not.

There is also a whole family of privacy laws — in Europe the big one is called GDPR (it stands for General Data Protection Regulation, but the name does not matter). Again, one plain idea: even public information about a real, living person has to be handled for a good reason, kept only as long as you need it, and not hoarded "just in case." You do not collect a mountain of details about a person because you can. You collect what you actually need for the actual question you are answering. That is called data minimisation, and it is just good manners with a fancy name — take only what is on your list.
section.subtitle: Consent, privacy, and the human on the other end
section.p: Behind every email address, every username, every blurry profile photo, there is a person. A real one. With a family, a bad day sometimes, feelings, a life. Keep that person in the room with you the entire time you work.

That single habit will keep you out of trouble more than any law will — because most wrong turns in OSINT do not come from not knowing the rules. They come from forgetting that the "target" is a human being.
So a few gentle standards:

• Have a reason. Before you look someone up, be able to say why. "I am curious" and "I want to build a file on my ex" are not reasons — they are red flags. A good reason is tied to a real, honest task.

• Do not pretend to be someone else to get information. Lying your way into data — telling a company you are the person's employer, for example — is called pretexting, and it is off-limits. Ask straight or do not ask.
• Do not contact and trick the person you are investigating. No fake friend requests to get past their privacy settings. No sweet-talking them into revealing things.
None of this makes you weak as an investigator. It makes you trusted. And in this field, being trusted is the whole career.
section.subtitle: When you do this for work — extra rules apply
section.p: Everything so far applies to everyone. But the moment you run OSINT for an organisation — vetting a job candidate, checking an employee, screening a partner — a second layer of rules switches on, and breaking them can be its own kind of trouble even when every source was public. You do not need to be a lawyer. You do need to know the tripwires exist and loop in the people who handle them.

• Hiring has its own laws. In the United States, using background information to make a hiring decision can pull you under the FCRA (Fair Credit Reporting Act) — with rules about permission and about telling the person before you act on what you found. And anti-discrimination law (the EEOC rules) means that if your search reveals someone's religion, health, pregnancy, age, or similar, and a decision then goes against them, the company can be accused of discriminating. The safe habit: record only job-relevant, verifiable facts — not everything you happened to see.

• Investigating your own people needs a documented reason. Regulated workplaces cannot just look up an employee "because." There has to be a legitimate, written purpose, and often HR or legal has to be in the loop first. Privacy laws like GDPR treat employee data with extra care. When in doubt, get authorisation before you start, not after.

• Faces and biometrics are special. Some places have specific laws about collecting or matching someone's face or other biometric data without consent. Treat face-search as a high-caution tool (we return to this later), and never run it on people at work without a legal check.

None of this is here to frighten you off. It is here so that the day your hobby skill gets used on the job, you already pause and ask, "Is there an extra rule because this is for an employer?" The answer is often yes.
section.subtitle: The special case: breach and leak data
section.p: You are going to hear a lot about breaches and leaks, so let me define them plainly. A breach is when a company gets hacked and its users' information spills out — sometimes including passwords. A leak is that spilled information floating around afterward. There are huge collections of this stuff on the internet.

This makes people nervous, and it should be handled with care. But there is a legal, useful, professional way to work with it — and there is a way that turns you into a criminal. The difference is, once again, one clean line.

cite.p: You may check whether something was exposed. You may never use a stolen password to get in.

section.p: • Checking exposure is fine. There are respected services that let you type in an email address and learn, "Yes, this email showed up in the such-and-such breach in 2019." That is a fact about exposure — like reading that a store had a burglary. Useful, honest, allowed. (The best-known service even refuses to hand you the passwords on purpose; it only tells you that you were exposed.)

• Using the stolen goods is not. Taking a leaked password and typing it into someone's email to see if it still works is walking through the front door. It is unauthorised access. It is a crime. It does not matter that the password was "just sitting there."

Professionals sometimes use a leaked password in one very specific, clever, safe way: as a fingerprint. If the exact same unusual password shows up attached to two different accounts, that is a strong hint the two accounts belong to the same person. Notice what happened there — the password was used to connect the dots, never to unlock a door. That is the entire game. Use identifiers to understand and link. Never to enter.

And one more honesty note about leak data: it is often old, messy, or flat-out wrong. A password from 2016 tells you about the past, not today. Never treat this stuff as gospel. Check it against a second source before you believe it.
section.subtitle: How to stay on the right side — a simple method
section.p: Run this routine before every single lookup. It takes thirty seconds and it will keep you clean for your whole career.
• Write down your reason. One honest sentence: "I am checking this business before signing a contract with them." If you cannot write the sentence, do not do the lookup.
• Ask: am I looking, or am I touching? If any step needs a password, a login, or getting past a lock — stop. Full stop. Find another, open path or do not go there.
• Ask: what did this person expect? Respect the original context. A public post to the world is fair. A private corner is not, even if you can reach it.
• Take only what you need. Do not vacuum up a person's whole life. Collect the few facts that answer your actual question. Skip the rest.
• Never pretend, never trick, never contact under a false face. No lying to get data. No fake accounts to befriend the subject.
• Keep honest notes as you go. Save the link, save the date, save what you saw — exactly as you saw it. (More on this in a moment.)
• Check anything important twice. One source is a rumour. Two independent sources start to be a fact.
Run those seven checks and you will almost never put a foot wrong.
section.subtitle: Keeping your notes honest
section.p: The notes deserve a moment of their own, because this is where good investigators separate themselves from sloppy ones — and it is also part of staying legal.

When you find something, write down where you found it, when you found it, and what it actually said — not what you wish it said, not your guess about what it means. Take a screenshot. Copy the exact web address. Note the date. Keep the fact and your opinion about the fact in two separate boxes.
Why does this matter so much? Two reasons.

First, honesty. If you blur "here is what I found" together with "here is what I think it means," you will fool yourself, and then you will fool whoever reads your work. Keep them apart. "The record says the company was registered three months ago" is a fact. "This is probably a fake company" is your opinion. Different boxes.

Second, protection. If your work is ever questioned — and one day it might be — your honest, dated, sourced notes are your shield. They show you looked at public things, in a public way, for a real reason. Good notes are the difference between "I found this out properly" and "trust me." Always be able to prove the first one.
section.subtitle: A short story: where a beginner slips and a pro stops
section.p: Here is a real-shaped situation. Everything and everyone in it is invented, but the choices are real. Follow the thinking.

Imagine you have been asked to check out a small vendor before your company signs a deal with them. The contact person is named Daniela Voss, and her email is daniela.voss@brightfield-supplies.com. Here is how it unfolds.

• Step 1 — The open look. You search the company name and find their website, their registration date, and a couple of news mentions. All public, all fair. You note the source and date for each. Good — you are firmly on the safe side.

• Step 2 — The exposure check. You run Daniela's email through a reputable breach-checking service. It tells you her email appeared in a leak two years ago. That is a fact about exposure. You write it down: "email exposed in [leak name], 2024." Still safe. You only learned that she was exposed, not anything secret.

• Step 3 — The temptation. The same leak is floating around online, and it includes passwords. A beginner thinks: "I could just check if her old password still logs into her email. It would tell me so much." This is the moment. This is the front door with the key under the mat.

• Step 4 — Where the pro stops. A professional does not even reach for the door handle. Logging in with that password would be unauthorised access — a crime — and it would poison the entire job. Even if you found something, it would be useless and illegal. So you stop. You note the exposure as a fact and move on. That is it. That is the whole difference between the beginner and the pro: the pro feels the line and steps back without drama.

• Step 5 — The clean finish. You keep working the open trails instead. You check the company's registration against the official public register. You look for public reviews and any public court records. You corroborate anything worrying with a second source. You write a calm, honest report: facts in one column, your assessment in another, every claim dated and sourced.
You see how that went? At no point did staying legal make you less effective. It made your work stronger, because everything in your report can stand up to daylight.
section.subtitle: The mindset: a pro knows where to stop
section.p: One idea ties this whole chapter together.

cite.p: A beginner asks, "Can I get this?" A professional asks, "Should I, and how far do I go?"

section.p: Knowing where to stop is not a limit on your skill. It is the skill. Anyone can be reckless; it takes a professional to move powerfully through public information and then, at exactly the right moment, step back from the locked door. That restraint is what makes people trust you with serious work, and it is what lets you sleep well.

I still remember the first time a trail led somewhere I had no business going. The question I had been asked was small and fair. But the path kept opening — a home, a family, a daily routine — and I could feel how easy the next step would be. I closed the file. Not because I could not take that step, but because taking it would have turned an honest inquiry into surveillance of a life. Walking away felt like losing. It was the most professional thing I did all year.
You now have the compass. The rest of this book is about learning to walk. Let us begin.
section.subtitle: Exercise
section.p: Here is a safe, legal exercise to make the bright line feel real.
• Pick a large public company you already know — a well-known brand, not a private person. Companies are public entities, so this keeps you far from any privacy concern.

• Spend fifteen minutes gathering only public facts: when it was founded, where it is headquartered, its official website, one or two recent news stories. For each item, write down the exact web address and the date you looked.
• Now write two short lists side by side. On the left: "Facts I found." On the right: "My opinion about what they mean." Keep them strictly separate. Feel how different those two columns are.
• Finally, write one honest sentence at the top of the page: your reason for looking. Practise the habit of never starting without it.
You just ran the whole method — reason first, public only, honest sourced notes, facts kept apart from opinion — on a target where you cannot possibly do harm. That is exactly how the pros warm up.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • The bright line is looking versus touching. Reading what is public is fine; logging into anything locked, or using a stolen password, is off-limits — always.
• Public does not mean anything-goes. Respect why and where something was shared, take only what you need, and remember there is a real person on the other end.
• A pro knows where to stop. Keep honest, dated, sourced notes, check important things twice, and treat stopping at the locked door as a skill — because it is the one that makes you trusted.

section.subtitle: Chapter Three
section.p: A small confession to start. The very first time I looked someone up online, I did it wrong.

I used my own account. My real name. My real photo. I opened the person's profile, poked around, and felt clever. Then, a few days later, that person showed up in my "People You May Know" list. The platform had quietly noticed I kept viewing them. It suggested us to each other. My cover — such as it was — was gone before I even knew I had a cover to lose.
Nobody got hurt that time. But it taught me the most important lesson in this whole book, and I want to give it to you before anything else.

p.strong: Before you look at anyone, protect yourself. Investigation is the second step. Safety is the first.

section.p: This chapter is about OPSEC. That word comes from the military. It means operational security — a fancy way of saying "don't leave a trail that points back to you." For us, it means one simple thing: you can look at the open internet without the open internet looking back at you.
Every idea here stays plain, and the setup is one you can build on a normal laptop this afternoon. No spy gadgets. No money required beyond a coffee's worth.
section.subtitle: Why you never investigate from your own accounts
section.p: The core idea. Say it out loud if it helps.

p.strong: Your real accounts are wired to your real life. The moment you use them to look, you risk showing your face to the person you're looking at.

section.p: Modern platforms — Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, all of them — are watching your behaviour as much as everyone else's. When you view a profile again and again, the platform notices. It may suggest you two to each other. On LinkedIn, the person can often see exactly who viewed them. One careless click and your name lands in their notifications.

There's a second danger, quieter but just as real. Your own account is full of you. Your friends. Your photos. Your workplace. Your habits. If the person you're researching is even a little curious, or a little dangerous, your account is a map straight to your front door. In OSINT, the person you study can sometimes study you back. Never hand them the map.
So we build a wall between "you the person" and "you the investigator." That wall is called a sock puppet.
section.subtitle: What a sock puppet is (and what it is not)
section.p: A sock puppet is a clean, research-only account. Think of it as a work glove. You put it on to handle things you don't want to touch with your bare hand. It has no link to your real name, your real email, your real photo, or your real phone. It exists for one job: looking, quietly.
The name comes from the old trick of putting a sock on your hand and pretending it's a different character. Same idea. It's a separate face you wear for research.
Beginners get into trouble on what a sock puppet is not, so be clear on it.

• It is not for tricking people into talking to you. We don't message the subject, friend them, or join their private groups uninvited — that crosses from looking into interacting, the line Chapter 2 drew.
• It is not a fake identity for scamming, catfishing, or harassment. Ever. If that's the goal, close this book.
• It is not a magic cloak. It hides your name. It does not, by itself, hide your location or your computer. We'll fix those separately.

The best sock puppets follow what missing-persons investigators call the no-touch rule: observe only. No likes. No comments. No friend requests. No password-reset probes. You are a fly on a public wall, nothing more.

p.strong: A sock puppet is a research-only account for watching the open web — never for contacting, tricking, or engaging anyone.

section.subtitle: Building your safe setup, step by step
section.p: Let's build the whole thing, in order. Do it once, keep it, and you'll have a clean research kit forever.

• Step 1 — Make a separate browser profile. You don't need a second computer. Most browsers (Firefox, Chrome, Brave) let you create a fresh profile — a totally separate browser space with its own history, cookies, and logins. Create one and name it something dull like "Research." Never open your personal accounts inside it, and never open your research accounts outside it. This one habit does most of the heavy lifting.

• Step 2 — Harden that browser a little. In the research profile, turn off telemetry (the browser phoning home about what you do). Block third-party cookies. Install a good ad-and-tracker blocker like uBlock Origin. These are free, take five minutes, and stop most of the invisible tracking that follows people around the web. (Tool names change over the years — the idea is "block trackers, kill cross-site cookies." Pick whatever reputable tool does that when you read this.)

• Step 3 — Understand what a browser leaks. Even with a blocker on, your browser quietly shows a lot: your operating system, your screen size, your fonts, your graphics chip. Together these make a fingerprint — a pattern almost as unique as a real fingerprint. A VPN does not hide this (more on VPNs in a moment). You don't need to become an expert today. Just know it exists, and keep all your research in that one browser profile so your "investigator self" always looks the same. Consistency is safer than chaos here.

• Step 4 — Create a brand-new email. Sign up for a fresh mailbox (Gmail, Proton, Outlook — any reputable one). Use it for nothing but research. This email must never have touched your real name, your real recovery phone, or your real accounts. It is the root of your sock puppet. Treat it like the key to the whole thing, because it is.

• Step 5 — Design the persona on paper first. Before you make any social account, decide who this puppet is. A plausible name. An age. A city. A boring job. A couple of harmless interests. Write it down and keep it consistent. A tool that generates random-but-realistic identities can seed this for you. The goal is forgettable and ordinary — someone nobody looks at twice.

• Step 6 — Handle phone verification honestly. Some platforms demand a phone number to sign up. Do not use your personal number — that instantly links the puppet to you. If you'll do this regularly, a cheap dedicated research SIM (a burner number kept only for this) is the clean answer. Free internet-phone numbers often get rejected, so a real SIM saves headaches.

• Step 7 — Pick a profile picture carefully. Never use a stock photo or a celebrity — a quick reverse-image search would burn you in seconds. Many people use an AI-generated face, but crop it and strip the hidden data (metadata) from the file first, because that data can quietly reveal where and how the image was made. Honestly, for pure passive watching, no photo at all is often fine.

• Step 8 — Age the account before you use it. A brand-new account is a red flag to platforms and people alike. Log in over a few days. Follow a few neutral pages — a sports team, a news site, a cooking group. Let it look lived-in. Then, and only then, go near your actual research. New accounts get locked fast; a warmed-up one survives.

• Step 9 — Never mix things. This is the golden thread through all of it. One email per puppet. One phone per puppet. Never reuse a photo, a password, or even a favourite turn of phrase across puppets or with your real self. Reuse is how investigators get linked — to each other and back to a real name. Keep everything in separate lanes.
That's the whole kit: separate browser profile, blocked trackers, fresh email, a thought-out persona, a clean phone if needed, a careful photo, and a warmed-up account. On a normal laptop. Today.
section.subtitle: What a VPN does — and the honest debate about it
section.p: You'll hear the word VPN everywhere in this world, so here it is, simply.

A VPN (virtual private network) hides your real internet address — your IP address, which is roughly the return address your connection stamps on everything you do. Without a VPN, the site you visit can see an address that points toward your home town and your internet provider. With a VPN, the site sees the VPN's address instead. It's like mailing a letter through a forwarding office so nobody reads your home street.
A few plain rules:
• Use a paid, reputable, no-logs VPN. "No-logs" means they don't keep records of what you did. Free VPNs make their money by selling your data — exactly the thing you're trying to protect. Skip them.
• A VPN hides your address, not your fingerprint. It is one layer, not the whole wall. This is why we bothered with the browser profile.
Now the honest part. Experienced investigators disagree about VPNs, and I want you to hear both sides rather than a slogan.
One camp says: always use a VPN. A clean address alone isn't enough against fingerprinting and location clues, so keep it on for everything.

The other camp says: turn the VPN off for the one moment you create an account. Why? Because some platforms recognise VPN addresses and treat them as suspicious at signup — they throw up puzzles, demand a phone number, or ban the new account outright.
Both camps are right, in context. Here's how I reconcile it in plain terms:

p.strong: Use your VPN for everyday looking and collecting. But for the delicate moment of creating a sock puppet on a picky platform, a clean, ordinary-looking home connection often works better than a VPN address the platform distrusts.

section.p: Don't memorise a rule. Understand the tradeoff: a VPN protects you, but a flagged VPN address can get your new account killed on sight. Judge each moment.
section.subtitle: Saving evidence honestly
section.p: Finding something is only half the job. If you can't prove what you found, and prove you didn't tamper with it, it may as well not exist. This matters double if your work could ever end up in a report, a dispute, or a court.
Here's the beginner-friendly version of doing it right:
• Capture the whole page, not a tiny crop. Save the full page with the web address (URL) visible and the date on screen. A lonely cropped screenshot with no context is easy to dismiss.

• Write down when and where. The exact date and time you saw it, the URL, and how you got there (what you searched, which platform). "I found it somewhere on Facebook" is worthless. "Viewed at this URL on this date at this time" is solid.
• Save it, don't just look at it. Content gets deleted. Save the page, and consider using a public web archive so there's an independent, dated copy you didn't control.
• Keep the original untouched. Don't crop, brighten, or "clean up" the saved evidence. If you need an edited version for a report, keep the untouched original too, and note that you edited a copy.
• Save the misses as well as the hits. If you searched and found nothing, record that too. It proves you looked, and it stops you from re-treading old ground.

As you grow, there are proper tools that capture pages automatically and stamp each one with a tamper-proof seal and a trusted timestamp — so nobody can accuse you of quietly changing a screenshot afterward. You don't need them on day one. You do need the habits above from your very first search.
section.subtitle: Simple note-taking so you never lose the thread
section.p: An investigation is a chain of small discoveries, and it is astonishingly easy to lose your place. Notes are how you hold the thread.

I learned this the hard way — by not doing it. I was once deep into a case with a conclusion I was sure of and no memory of how I reached it. I could not retrace a single step, so I had to throw the whole thing out and start over. A finding you cannot walk someone else back through is not a finding — it is a feeling. Since that day I have written down every click, in order, before I let myself believe anything.
Keep it dead simple. One note file per case. For every finding, jot four things: what you found, where (the URL or source), when you found it, and how (the search or tool). And keep one line sacred:

p.strong: Separate what you saw from what you think it means. Facts in one column, your guesses in another. Never let them blur.

section.p: That last habit is the difference between a professional and someone who fools themselves. "His profile lists Kyiv" is a fact. "So he probably lives in Kyiv" is a guess. Write both, but never confuse them. Also record your dead ends and the reasons you dropped a lead — future-you will thank present-you.
section.subtitle: A beginner slip, and the fix
section.p: Here is a short, made-up story that could happen to anyone.
Meet Daria Kovalenko, a beginner, curious and eager. A friend asks her to check whether a marketplace seller named Roman Petrenko is trustworthy — a small favour, or so it seems.

• Step 1 — The slip. Daria opens Instagram in her normal browser, logged in as her real self, and views Roman's profile. Twice. She also clicks a link he posted, which loads a page that quietly records visitors. She feels productive.

• Step 2 — The exposure. A day later, Roman's account shows up as a suggested friend for Daria — and hers for him. Because she was logged in as herself, her real name and photo were the "visitor" the platform tied to those profile views. Roman now knows a woman named Daria Kovalenko has been looking at him. Her real face. Her real friends list, one click away.

• Step 3 — The fix, part one. Daria stops. She creates a separate "Research" browser profile and never touches her personal accounts inside it. She installs a tracker blocker. From now on, her looking and her real life live in different rooms.

• Step 4 — The fix, part two. She makes a fresh email, invents a plain, boring persona named Olena Marchuk, and builds a lightweight sock-puppet account. She warms it up for a few days with neutral follows. She keeps her VPN on for browsing.

• Step 5 — The fix, part three. Now she views Roman's public profile through the puppet, in the research browser. She saves the full page with the URL and date, notes what she found versus what she suspects, and — crucially — never messages him. Observe only.
Same task. Same laptop. The difference is a wall between Daria-the-person and the eyes doing the looking. That wall is the whole chapter.
section.subtitle: Exercise
section.p: Build your kit before you ever need it. This should take under an hour and costs nothing but a fresh email.
1. Create a separate browser profile just for research. Name it plainly.
2. In it, install a reputable tracker blocker and turn off telemetry and third-party cookies.
3. Create a brand-new email that has never touched your real identity.
4. On paper, design one ordinary persona: name, age, city, a boring job, two harmless interests. Keep it forgettable.
5. Visit a "what does my browser reveal" test page and simply read what your research browser leaks. Don't fix anything yet — just look, so the idea of a fingerprint feels real.
6. Open a plain note file and practise logging one harmless, public thing (say, a museum's opening hours) using the four fields: what, where, when, how — and add one line separating fact from guess.
You've now built the wall and the notebook. Everything else in this book stands on top of them.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • Safety comes first, always. Never investigate from your own accounts — build a wall between you-the-person and you-the-investigator using a separate browser profile and a research-only sock puppet.
• A sock puppet is for watching, not touching. Fresh email, plain persona, clean phone if needed, careful photo, warmed-up account — and never reuse anything across puppets or with your real self.

• Work honestly and keep the thread. Use a reputable VPN (but understand the signup debate), save full-page evidence with URL and date, keep originals untouched, and take simple notes that separate what you saw from what you think.

section.subtitle: Chapter Four
section.p: Most people search badly. That is not an insult. It is just the truth, and I include my younger self in it. We type a few words into a search box, glance at the first page, and give up if the answer is not staring back at us. The search engine did exactly what we asked. We simply asked a vague question, so we got a vague answer.

This chapter fixes that. By the end of it you will search on purpose. You will tell the engine precisely what you want and, just as importantly, what you do not want. You will learn a small set of commands — we call them operators — that turn a wide, messy search into a narrow, sharp one. And you will learn "dorking," a word that sounds mysterious and is not. It just means searching carefully.
Everything here uses public search engines the way they were built to be used. Just skill.
section.subtitle: The one big idea: precision beats volume
section.p: Almost everyone makes the same mistake. They think more results are better — that a search returning two million pages is a success.

It is the opposite. Two million results means the engine did not understand you. It threw everything vaguely related into a pile and left you to dig. A great search often returns five results — and the answer is in the first one.

cite.p: Your goal is not more results. Your goal is the right results.

section.p: It works like fishing. A beginner drags a huge net through the whole ocean and hauls up mostly seaweed. A professional knows the exact spot, the exact bait, the exact depth — and catches the one fish they came for. Operators are your bait and your depth gauge.

One key term first, because I will use it constantly. An operator is a special word or symbol you add to your search that gives the engine an extra instruction. Normal words say what to look for. Operators say how and where to look. That is the whole secret.
section.subtitle: The operators, one at a time
section.p: Each one comes with a tiny example. Read them slowly and, if you can, type each into a search engine as you go. You learn this in your fingers, not just your eyes. Throughout, I use made-up names, handles, and websites so nothing here points at a real person.
section.subtitle: Exact match — quotation marks
section.p: Put words inside "quotation marks" and the engine must find those exact words, in that exact order. Without quotes, the engine feels free to shuffle your words around, swap in synonyms, and drop words it thinks are unimportant.
• Marina Delcroix — the engine may show pages with "Marina," pages with "Delcroix," and pages that only loosely match.
• "Marina Delcroix" — only pages with that full name, spelled that way, side by side.
This is the single most useful habit in searching. Names, phrases, error messages, quotes from a speech — wrap them in quotes and watch the noise fall away.
section.subtitle: Search inside one website — site:
section.p: The site: operator tells the engine to look only within one website. You type site: then the web address, no space.
• site:linkedin.com "Marina Delcroix" — find that name only on LinkedIn.
• site:reddit.com stolen bicycle Copenhagen — search Reddit alone.

This is powerful for two reasons. First, a website's own search box is often weak, while a search engine has already indexed that whole site far better. Second, you can aim at exactly the corner of the internet where your answer probably lives.
You can even point site: at a whole type of website by using the ending of the address:
• site:gov.uk — only British government pages.
• site:.edu — only educational institutions, mostly universities. (Note the leading dot: site:.edu matches the whole .edu family, not a single site.)
section.subtitle: Find specific file types — filetype:
section.p: Not everything on the internet is a normal web page. Reports, spreadsheets, presentations, and forms are often documents. The filetype: operator finds them.
• filetype:pdf "annual report" Meridian Logistics — find PDF reports for a made-up company.
• filetype:xlsx budget 2024 site:gov.uk — find spreadsheets (xlsx is an Excel file) on UK government sites.
• filetype:pptx "Meridian Logistics" — find PowerPoint slide decks that name the company.

Documents are gold. People are careful about what they put on a web page but often forget what is buried in an old PDF or a spreadsheet that got posted years ago. A phone list, a staff directory, meeting minutes — these hide in documents.
section.subtitle: Look in the title or the web address — intitle: and inurl:
section.p: Every web page has a title (the headline that shows in the browser tab) and an address (the URL, the www... line at the top). Two operators let you search inside just those parts.

• intitle:"staff directory" Meridian Logistics — pages whose title contains "staff directory." A page bothering to title itself that is very likely the real thing, not a page that merely mentions it in passing.
• inurl:careers site:meridianlogistics.example — pages whose address contains the word "careers."

Why does this matter? Because a keyword in the title or the address is a strong signal that the page is about that thing, not just brushing past it. It is a way of finding pages that are on-target rather than tangentially related.
section.subtitle: Remove what you do not want — the minus sign
section.p: Put a minus sign - directly in front of a word (no space) and the engine will throw out every page containing that word. This is how you clean up a messy search.
• jaguar -car -animal — you want the guitar amplifier or the sports team, not the car and not the big cat.
• "Marina Delcroix" -obituary — you are looking for the living person and keep hitting a funeral notice for someone with the same name. Remove it.
• Meridian Logistics -jobs -careers — you want news and records about the company, not endless job postings.
The minus sign is quiet but mighty. Most bad searches are not missing the right pages — they are drowning them under the wrong ones. Subtract the wrong ones.
section.subtitle: Widen the net on purpose — OR
section.p: Sometimes you want either of two things. Type OR in capital letters between them. (Capitals matter; lowercase "or" is treated as a normal word.)
• "Marina Delcroix" OR "M. Delcroix" — catch both the full name and the shortened form.
• Meridian Logistics (invoice OR receipt OR statement) — the round brackets group the choices neatly.
Use OR when your target might be written more than one way — a nickname, an abbreviation, a maiden name, a spelling variant. You are telling the engine, "any of these will do."
section.subtitle: Fill in the blank — the wildcard
section.p: The asterisk * is a wildcard. It means "something goes here, I do not know exactly what." It works best inside a quoted phrase.
• "Marina * Delcroix" — finds "Marina Anne Delcroix," "Marina J. Delcroix," and so on. The * stands in for the missing middle name.
• "chief * officer" site:meridianlogistics.example — finds "chief executive officer," "chief financial officer," "chief technology officer," all at once.
The wildcard is your friend when you know the shape of a phrase but not every word in it.
section.subtitle: Narrow by time — date filters
section.p: Old results can bury fresh ones, and sometimes you specifically want old ones. Every major search engine has a date filter, usually tucked under a "Tools" or "Filters" button beneath the search box. Set it to the last year, the last month, or a custom range.
On some engines you can also filter by date right in the query with before: and after: using year-month-day:
• Meridian Logistics after:2023-01-01 before:2023-12-31 — only results from the year 2023.
Dates matter more than beginners expect. A merger, a name change, a scandal — knowing when something happened lets you slice straight to the reporting from that window.
section.subtitle: Use more than one search engine
section.p: One habit separates the pros from everyone else: they never trust a single search engine.

Google, Bing, and Yandex do not show the same results. Each one crawls the web differently, ranks pages differently, and — crucially — censors and prioritises differently based on where its company sits.
• Google is the broadest for most of the world and the one most people know.
• Bing (Microsoft's engine) often surfaces pages Google buries, and its image search behaves differently, which sometimes helps.

• Yandex is a Russian engine and is far stronger for content in Russian and for many things in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. It is also famously good at reverse image search — but that is a later chapter.

cite.p: Different engines see different internets. If one shows you nothing, another may show you everything.

section.p: The good news: the core operators — quotes, site:, filetype:, the minus sign — work across all three, with only small differences. So the skill you just learned travels. When a search comes up empty on Google, do not conclude the answer is not out there. Run the same query on Bing and Yandex before you give up. I have cracked more than one case simply by moving the exact same search to a different engine.
section.subtitle: So what is "Google dorking"?
section.p: You have probably heard the phrase "Google dorking" and maybe it sounded like hacking. It is not.

A "dork" is just a precise search that stacks several operators together. That is all. The word came from security researchers, but the technique is nothing more than what you have already learned in this chapter, combined. When someone writes a clever query like site:meridianlogistics.example filetype:pdf "employee handbook", that is "a dork." It is skilled searching, not sneaking.

Finding a document that a website put on the open internet is legal and normal — a search engine indexing a public file makes reading it no different from reading any other public page. The line Chapter 2 drew still holds: the operator is neutral, and it is your intent and actions that matter. If a search accidentally surfaces something clearly sensitive that was exposed by error, the right move is to note it, not exploit it, and where appropriate report it.

cite.p: A dork is a precise question. Asking a precise question is never the crime. What you do with the answer can be.

section.subtitle: A worked case: finding one person, the professional way
section.p: Watch the operators combine into something real. A fictional request: a colleague asks me to confirm the current employer and professional background of a person they only know as Marina Delcroix, who they believe works somewhere in the logistics industry in Europe. A name and a hunch — that is all we have. Watch how each operator narrows the fog.

• Step 1 — Lock the name. I never search a name without quotes. I start with "Marina Delcroix" in Google. A pile of loosely related results comes back, including, annoyingly, an obituary for a different Marina Delcroix and dozens of unrelated social posts. That pile tells me the name exists and is not vanishingly rare. Good enough to begin.
section.subtitle: What that first, noisy page looks like

p.code: — 3 of top 4 are noise; only #4 is on-topic

section.p: • Step 2 — Cut the noise. I remove the wrong person and the wrong context: "Marina Delcroix" -obituary -funeral. The death notice vanishes. The results are cleaner already. Precision is mostly subtraction.

• Step 3 — Go where professionals live. Logistics is a career, so I aim at the professional network: site:linkedin.com "Marina Delcroix" logistics. Now I get a small handful of profiles instead of the whole internet. The top profile looks perfect — a Marina Delcroix, and the word "logistics" is right there. It would be easy to stop and call it a match. But I read past the headline, and the friction shows: this Marina Delcroix does supply-chain software sales, based in Montreal, and "logistics" is just a keyword in her pitch. Wrong person. The engine matched my words, not my target. A first-page result that fits your query is not the same as a result that fits your case.

• Step 4 — Reframe, then confirm with a second source. So I stop trusting the top hit and tighten the query with the one detail I actually have — Europe: site:linkedin.com "Marina Delcroix" logistics (Europe OR Rotterdam OR Antwerp). This time a different profile rises: a Marina Delcroix in operations at a firm I will call Meridian Logistics, based in the right part of the world. That is a lead, not a fact — so I corroborate it before I believe it. I never trust one page, so I search the company's own site for her name: site:meridianlogistics.example "Marina Delcroix". A team page and a press release both name her as a regional operations manager. Now an independent source agrees with the profile, and the Montreal false hit is behind me.

• Step 5 — Reach for the documents. Web pages get scrubbed; documents get forgotten. I run "Marina Delcroix" Meridian filetype:pdf. A conference programme from 2023 lists her as a speaker, with a short professional biography — exactly the background detail my colleague asked for. That biography also mentions a previous employer, which is a fresh thread I could pull if I needed to.

• Step 6 — Check a second engine. Before I write anything up, I run the two best queries again on Bing and Yandex. Bing surfaces a local news article Google had buried, which quotes her by name and title. Now three separate, public sources agree on employer and role. I stop here, because the question is answered and everything traces back to a public page I can cite.

Notice what happened. I never guessed. Each step used a plain operator you now know, and each step either narrowed the search or added an independent confirmation. That is the whole craft in miniature.

And notice the deeper lesson: good searching is itself the first pivot. In OSINT, a "pivot" means using one fact you have found to reach the next fact. A precise search does not just answer your question — it hands you new threads (a previous employer, a co-author, an old address) that become the starting point of your next search. You are not just finding an answer. You are opening doors.
section.subtitle: Exercise
section.p: Pick a made-up target you can safely play with, or use a public figure you have permission and reason to look up for practice — a well-known author, for instance. Then do the following, writing down the query and the number of results at each step so you can see precision at work:
1. Search their full name with no quotes. Note roughly how many results come back.
2. Search the same name inside quotes. Did the number drop? Did the top results get more relevant?
3. Add a site: operator to search only one platform where they are likely to appear.
4. Add a minus sign to remove one kind of result that is getting in your way.
5. Run a filetype:pdf search for their name and see whether any documents surface that the normal web pages did not show.
6. Finally, take your single best query and run it, unchanged, on Bing and Yandex as well as Google. Write down one result that appeared on one engine but not the others.
If you finish and your last search returns fewer, sharper results than your first — congratulations. You have stopped dragging a net through the ocean.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • Precision beats volume. A search that returns five right pages beats one that returns two million wrong ones. Operators — quotes, site:, filetype:, intitle:/inurl:, the minus sign, OR, the wildcard *, and date filters — are how you get there.

• Stack operators and switch engines. A "dork" is nothing but several operators combined into one precise, legal question. And because Google, Bing, and Yandex see different internets, running the same query on all three is often the difference between empty-handed and answered.

• Good searching is the first pivot. Each sharp search not only answers today's question but hands you the next thread to pull — always confirmed against a second independent public source before you believe it.

section.subtitle: Chapter Five
section.p: Here is the day a username unravelled a whole life.

I once had almost nothing to work with. One handle. Seven little letters that a person had typed into a signup box years ago and forgotten about. No real name. No photo I trusted. No location. Just that string.

Two hours later I had a full name, three email addresses, a home city, and a face. I did not hack anything. I did not break a single law. I just pulled on one thread, and the whole sweater came apart.
That thread was a username. And in this chapter I am going to teach you how to pull it.
section.subtitle: What a username actually is
section.p: A username is the name a person picks for themselves online. It is also called a handle. It is the @something on Twitter or Instagram. It is the name in front of a Reddit account. It is the part of an email before the @ sign.

People choose these names once, when they are young or in a hurry, and then they keep them. Forever. That is the secret. A username feels small and throwaway. It is not. It is one of the strongest starting clues in all of open-source intelligence.

Open-source intelligence, or OSINT, just means finding things out using information that is already public — only what people have left in the open, where anyone is allowed to look (the boundary Chapter 2 set). We collect it, we connect it, and we reason carefully about what it means.
A username is the perfect first thread for one plain reason.

cite.p: People are lazy with names. They reuse the same handle everywhere.

section.p: Look at your own life. You probably have one or two nicknames you have typed into a hundred signup forms. Maybe it is a childhood nickname. Maybe it is your name plus a favourite number. Maybe it is a word you liked when you were fourteen. And you have used it on gaming sites, forums, shopping accounts, and social media, over and over, for years.
Everyone does this. It is human. Making up a fresh clever name every single time is tiring, and people are tired. So they reuse. And that reuse is a trail.
section.subtitle: The core idea
section.p: The whole chapter in one sentence:
If a person uses the same rare username in many places, you can walk from one place to the next and slowly build a picture of who they are.
That is it. One handle becomes a map. Each stop on the map gives you something new: a photo, a real name, a linked email, another handle, a city. And each new thing lets you take another step.
But there is a rule I need you to burn into your mind before we go one inch further. It is the most important sentence in this book.

cite.p: Matching names do NOT prove same person.

section.p: Two accounts with the same handle might be one human. Or they might be two strangers who happened to pick the same word. Or a name someone abandoned and a stranger later grabbed. The match is a lead, not a conclusion. A lead is a hint that points somewhere. A conclusion is something you have actually proven. Never confuse the two. This is the mistake that ruins beginners, and it is the single sentence to carry out of this chapter.

I learned it the embarrassing way. Early on, I was certain I had my man. Same rare handle, same city, the timeline fit. I wrote his name at the top of my notes and felt clever. I was wrong. It was a stranger who happened to share the handle — the trail had forked two profiles earlier, and I walked past it because I wanted to be right. That miss taught me more than any clean hit ever did: the moment you start hoping a clue points at your target, you have stopped investigating and started guessing.
section.subtitle: The confidence ladder
section.p: Since matching names do not prove identity, we need a way to talk about how sure we are. I use a simple ladder. Every clue you find sits on one of these rungs.
• Weak. A single shared handle. A common avatar. A generic bio. On its own, this proves almost nothing. Especially if the handle is short or ordinary, like john or mike88.
• Moderate. A rare, unusual handle reused, plus something else that fits. Same account age. Some overlapping friends. Now you are getting somewhere.
• Strong. A truly rare signal lines up. The exact same unusual profile photo file. The exact same odd phrase in two bios. A recovery hint that matches. Two of these together and you are almost there.
• Confirmed. The subject links the accounts themselves ("find me on X"). Or a hard identifier, like a recovery email fragment, points to one and only one person.

Your job as an investigator is to climb this ladder. You start at the bottom with a weak lead. You gather more clues. Each clue that fits pulls you up a rung. You do not name a real human until you are near the top.
The rarer the clue, the faster you climb. A common handle barely moves you. A one-of-a-kind handle plus a one-of-a-kind photo can carry you most of the way in two steps.
section.subtitle: The method, step by step
section.p: This is how I work a username from scratch. Follow the order.
• Get your seed. The one handle you start with is your seed. Write it down exactly, letter for letter. Case usually does not matter, but spelling always does.

• Check where it exists. Take the seed and look for it across many platforms at once. This is called enumeration — a big word that just means "checking a list." You are asking: on which sites does this exact handle resolve to a real, live profile? There are free tools that check hundreds of sites in seconds — well-known examples are Sherlock, Maigret, and WhatsMyName (tool names change over time, so treat these as examples, not gospel). But remember: the tool only tells you a page exists. It does not tell you the page is your person. You still look with your own eyes.

• Triage the hits by hand. Triage means sorting results by what matters. Open each live hit. Is it a real profile with real activity, or an empty placeholder? Some sites show a "taken" page for a name nobody really uses. That is a false hit. Throw it out.
• Harvest new threads. On every real profile, collect anything new: a real name, a bio, a linked website, a photo, another handle they mention, a city. Each new item is a fresh thread to pull.
• Follow the threads. Feed the new handles back into enumeration. Feed a real name into the next step, permutations. Feed a photo into image search. Round and round, the picture grows.

• Rank every link on the ladder. As you go, keep asking: how sure am I that this account is the same person? Write the rung down. Weak, moderate, strong, confirmed. Do not let a weak lead quietly turn into a fact in your head.
Three of those steps deserve opening up, because they are where beginners find the real gold.
section.subtitle: Guessing the variations
section.p: People do not always reuse a handle exactly. Sometimes they change it a little. firecat becomes fire_cat becomes firecat88 becomes thefirecat. The trick is that each person changes it in their own consistent way. This is their personal naming grammar — their private rulebook for making handles.
Once you spot the rulebook, you can predict handles you have not even found yet.
To generate variations, take the parts you know and mix them:
• First name and last name in different orders: annalee, anna.lee, leeanna, a_lee.
• Add a number they seem to like, or a birth year: annalee92, anna_lee_1992.
• Swap letters for look-alikes, called leetspeak: e to 3, o to 0, so annalee becomes ann4l33.
• Add the small words they favour: theannalee, realannalee, annaleexo.
Then run those guesses back through enumeration to see which ones are real. Predicting a handle feels clever, but a prediction sits on the weak rung until a live profile proves it real.
section.subtitle: Turning a username into an email, and back
section.p: The part of an email before the @ is called the local-part. In annalee92@gmail.com, the local-part is annalee92. Notice something? That is a handle. So emails and usernames flow into each other.
• Email to username. If you find an email, strip off the local-part and run it through enumeration like any other handle. annalee92 might be on ten sites.

• Username to email. If you have a handle, guess emails from it. Try annalee92@gmail.com, annalee92@outlook.com, annalee92@proton.me. Then confirm which mailboxes actually exist using an existence check.

An existence check asks a website, in a gentle and public way, "does an account with this email exist here?" Many sites answer that quietly, without ever bothering the account owner. Free tools do this for you across dozens of services. A word of care: a few sites will send the owner a notice if you poke them. Avoid those, or you tip off your subject and cross a line you should not cross. Stay on the public, quiet side of the fence.
How well this pivot works depends entirely on how rare the local-part is. annalee92 pivots beautifully. info or contact or admin tells you nothing, because a million people use them.
section.subtitle: The photo is a second thread
section.p: A username is thread number one. A profile photo, the avatar, is thread number two. And it is often stronger, because people reuse images even more carelessly than they reuse names.
Two ways to pull this thread:

• Reverse image search. You give a search engine the picture instead of words, and it finds other places that exact picture appears. If the same odd photo shows up on three accounts with three different handles, that is a strong sign one person runs all three.
• Face search. Some engines find the same face across different photos. That is even more powerful, because it can link a person even when they used a different picture each time.
But hold the ladder in mind here too.

• Similar is not identical. A result that merely looks like your photo may be a different crop, a re-post, or a genuine look-alike. Before you trust a match, confirm it is the same image — not just a similar one.
• A rare, original photo the person took themselves is a strong signal.
• A stock photo, a celebrity, or a picture thousands of people use is worth nothing for identity.
• An AI-generated face — a fake face made by a computer — will return no matches at all. And that silence is its own signal. A face that exists nowhere else is often a made-up persona.

p.strong: Do not use face-search tools without written authorisation and a legal check.

section.p: Face-search touches people's privacy directly, and in many places it is restricted or outright illegal. Know the rules where you are, get permission in writing, and have a clear lawful reason before you ever run one. This is not optional — it is the one pivot in this chapter that can put you on the wrong side of the law.
section.subtitle: One case, start to finish
section.p: Watch the whole thing work, on a made-up person. Everyone and everything here is invented. Follow the pulls — and notice how little I have to start with.

• Step 1 — The seed. A small online shop is getting fake five-star reviews. Every fake review comes from an account with the handle mossyfern. That is all I have. One handle, seven letters, nothing else. I write it down: mossyfern.
• Step 2 — Enumeration. I run mossyfern across a few hundred sites. The tool does not hand me a clean list. Here is roughly what it actually prints:
section.subtitle: What a username enumerator prints
section.p: Read that honestly. The tool leans optimistic — it counts a page as "found" the moment it loads, even a parked one, so those green lines are hits to check, not leads to trust. Instagram, the one platform I most wanted, has no mossyfern at all. That is not a bug; the handle simply is not there, and I write that down. Right now this whole run is a weak lead.

• Step 3 — Triage and harvest. I open each hit with my own eyes, because the tool only proved a page loads. The recipe site is an empty placeholder — the name is taken, but there are no posts, no avatar, nothing. That is a false hit; the tool called it "found" and it is really just a parked, generic page. I throw it out. The Twitter hit is the dangerous one: it is a real, busy account, but it belongs to a teenage boy in another country posting about football. Same seven letters, completely different human. This is the classic false positive — someone else grabbed the identical handle. I catch it not by the name (the name matched perfectly) but by the content, the photos, and the dates: nothing there touches plants, houses, or a rainy city, and the account is three years newer than the others. Out it goes. Two hits survive. The photo site is real and active: dozens of pictures of houseplants, and a bio that reads "plant mom in the rainy city, she/her." The gaming forum is real too, and the profile links out to a personal blog. Two real profiles. I harvest: a hobby (plants), a hint of location (rainy city), a linked blog.

cite.p: Same seven letters, different human. That is the homonym trap in the flesh.

section.p: • Step 4 — The avatar pull. Both real profiles use the same photo: a woman holding a fern by a window. I reverse-image-search it. The exact same photo appears on a small local plant-club page, captioned "our volunteer Deborah Ashworth." Now I have a possible real name. This is a strong signal — a rare, original photo tying the handle to a name. I have climbed two rungs at once.

• Step 5 — Permutations from the name. With "Deborah Ashworth" in hand, I build variations: deborahashworth, dashworth, deb_ashworth, debashworth. I run them back through enumeration. deb_ashworth is live on a professional networking site, listing a job at a plant nursery in the city of Elmbrook. "Rainy city" and "Elmbrook" and "plants" all fit. Moderate signal on its own, but it stacks neatly on what I already have.

• Step 6 — The email pivot. From the blog I found in Step 3, the "contact" page shows deb.ashworth.ferns@gmail.com. I do not email it. I run a quiet existence check. That address is registered on the photo site and the gaming forum — the exact two accounts I started with. That is a strong signal, but I stop myself: it is one check. One positive result, however clean, earns strong and no higher. It stays strong until a second, independent source agrees. So I hold it there and go looking for that second source.

• Step 7 — Confirm and stop. I already have it. The rare original photo tied the handle to the name Deborah Ashworth on the plant-club page (Step 4). The email check now ties the same handle to the same name a second, independent way (Step 6). Two separate sources, arrived at by two separate paths, point to one person. That is what lifts me from strong to confirmed — not the email alone, but the email plus the photo agreeing. I write up the finding with each rung of evidence laid out plainly, so anyone can check my work. And then I stop. I do not chase her private life beyond the question I was asked. That restraint is part of the craft.

Look back at what happened. Each step handed the next step its fuel. Handle led to profiles. Profiles led to a photo. Photo led to a name. Name led to more handles. Handles led to an email. Email closed the loop. No single clue proved anything. All of them together did.

And notice the mess I did not skip past. The tool called a parked recipe page "found," so I opened it and binned it. It matched a stranger on Twitter, so I killed the false positive by reading content and dates, not the name. Real work looks like this.
section.subtitle: The traps that catch beginners
section.p: Before you go practise, learn the mistakes so you can dodge them.

• The homonym trap. Two different people, same handle. This is the most common failure of all. Short and common handles are almost worthless because so many people share them. Trust rare strings, doubt common ones.

• The recycled name. Someone abandons a handle; a stranger grabs it later. The old posts and the new posts are two different humans wearing the same name. Verify that the person continued, not just the string.

• The tool that lies. Enumeration tools break as websites change. They report hits that are not real and miss hits that are. Always look with your own eyes, and run more than one tool, because each checks a different list of sites.
• The fake face. A stock photo or an AI face links nothing to a real identity. Do not build a case on a picture anyone could use.
Every one of these traps has the same cure: climb the ladder and gather independent clues.
section.subtitle: Exercise
section.p: Do this on yourself. It is the safest and most eye-opening way to learn.
• Write down the oldest username you can remember using — the one from your teenage years, the one you typed everywhere without thinking.

• Run it through a free cross-platform username checker. (A note on tools: some are just websites you open; others are small free programs you install, sometimes run from a terminal. If a terminal is new to you, start with a browser-based checker — the method is identical, and you never need to pay to practise anything in this book.) See how many places it still lives.
• Open each real hit. Ask: what could a stranger learn about me from this alone? A hobby? A city? A real name? An old photo?
• Now try three variations of that handle, using your own naming grammar. How many are also you?
• Finally, take the oldest profile photo you can find of yourself and reverse-image-search it. Where else does it appear?
Sit with what you find. This is exactly what someone would do to a target. Feeling it from the inside teaches you both how the method works and why we treat it with such care.

cite.p: Turn it around. The fix for everything you just found on yourself: stop reusing one handle everywhere, retire old accounts you no longer touch, and keep your real name off throwaway profiles. That single reused username is the thread that ties your whole life together — cut it. (Full checklist: Appendix D, "Take it back.")

section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • A username is often the single best starting thread, because people reuse the same handle across many sites for years, and one handle leads to another, then to photos, names, and emails.

• Work the thread in order: enumerate where the handle exists, triage the real hits by eye, harvest new clues, guess variations, and pivot between username and email — with the profile photo as a strong second thread.
• Matching names never prove same person. Climb the confidence ladder from weak to confirmed, stack independent clues, watch for homonyms and recycled names, and stay strictly legal and open-source.

section.subtitle: Chapter Six
