section.p: Your own email address — count how many places you typed it this year. A shopping site. A newsletter. A new app. A work login. A game your kid wanted. A dentist's booking form.

Now consider how long you have had that address. Many people keep the same email for ten years, some for twenty. We change our phone number when we switch carriers. We move house. We change jobs. But the email stays.
That is why, in OSINT, the email address is the master key.

Quick reminder of the word. OSINT means Open-Source Intelligence. It is the craft of finding facts about a person or thing using only information that is already public — the open web, public records, things people posted themselves. No hacking. No tricks that break the law. Just careful looking.

An email address is one small string of text. But it is a stable, unique label for one person. Stable means it rarely changes. Unique means only one person uses it. Put those two together and you have something rare: a single dot that connects to dozens of other dots. Where the person shops. What apps they use. What their real name is. Sometimes their photo. Sometimes an old password habit they never fixed.
In this chapter I will show you how to pull on that string — gently, legally, and step by step.

cite.p: An email address is the one label a person carries for years across the whole internet. Find it, and doors start to open.

section.subtitle: Why an email ties so much together
section.p: Every account you make asks for an email. It has to. That is how the site says "you are you" when you log back in. That is how it sends you a receipt or a reset link.
So your email quietly becomes a list of everywhere you have been. Not on purpose. It just happens.
For an investigator, that means one email can answer questions like:
• Which websites and apps is this person signed up on?
• What is their real name?
• What username do they like to use?
• Has their data ever leaked in a hack — and if so, from which service?
• Is this the same person as that other account I found?
We will take these one at a time. But first, the rule that keeps you safe and honest.
section.subtitle: The line you never cross
section.p: There is a bright, clear line in email OSINT. Learn it now and it will protect you your whole career.

p.strong: You may check whether an account exists. You may never touch the account.

section.p: Checking is fine. Asking a website "is there an account here for this email?" is a public question anyone can ask. Reading what the website chooses to show you is fine.

Touching is not fine. Logging in is not fine. Guessing a password is not fine. Using a leaked password to get inside an account — even to "just look" — is not fine. That is not OSINT. It is breaking in, and in most countries it is a crime.

The simplest way to hold it in your head: picture standing on the pavement outside a house. You are allowed to notice the lights are on, the car is in the drive, the mailbox says "Karas." You are not allowed to open the door. Same street, different act.

cite.p: Confirm that an account exists. Read what the site volunteers. Then stop. Never log in, never guess, never use a leaked password.

section.p: We will come back to this line more than once, because it matters most where the temptation is strongest.
section.subtitle: Method 1 — Where is this email used?
section.p: The first thing you want from an email is a map. Where is this person signed up?
There is a clever, gentle way to find out, and it uses a feature every website already has: the "forgot password" and "sign up" forms.

The idea, in plain words: when you go to a website and start the "forgot password" flow, the site has to ask itself: do we have an account for this email? And then it usually tells you the answer, right there on the screen, before you have proved anything.
• If it says "we've sent a reset link to your email" or "that email is already in use" — an account exists.
• If it says "we couldn't find an account with that email" — no account.
That difference in wording is called a differential. It is just a fancy word for "the site gives two different answers, and the answer tells you what you want to know."

Notice what you did not do. You did not log in. You did not get the reset link (that goes to the target's inbox, not yours). You did not touch anything. You asked a public question and read the answer. That is why this technique is on the safe side of the line. But be honest about what "passive" means: it means you did not log in — not that you are invisible. A site can rate-limit these checks, log the attempt, or count it as a breach of its terms of service. Quiet is not the same as undetectable.
You could do this by hand, one website at a time — click "forgot password," type the email, read the answer, write it down. Doing it a few times by hand teaches you what the answers look like.

There are also tools that check many sites at once and hand you a list. Their names come and go, so I will not marry you to any one of them. A well-known free one has been Holehe, which checks over a hundred sites and reports whether the email is registered on each; a hosted service called Epieos does something similar in your browser. Treat these as examples of the method, not as gospel. Email tools rot fast — they depend on other websites' forms, and those forms change every month. Always cross-check a surprising "not found" with a second tool before you believe it.
What you get at the end is gold: a footprint. "This email is on GitHub, Spotify, and an old forum." Each is a new thread to pull.
section.subtitle: Method 2 — Turning a name into an email (the pattern trick)
section.p: Sometimes you have the opposite problem. You know a person's name and where they work, but you do not have their email. You want to work it out.

One key fact makes this possible. Companies almost always follow one pattern for everyone. They do not invent a new style for each employee — that would be chaos for their IT team. So they pick one recipe and stamp it on the whole company.
Common recipes look like this. Say the company domain is brightmail.com and the employee is Jason Karas:
• first.last → jason.karas@brightmail.com
• flast (first initial + last name) → jkaras@brightmail.com
• first → jason@brightmail.com
• f.last → j.karas@brightmail.com
• firstl → jasonk@brightmail.com
And here is the beautiful part, worth saying out loud:

cite.p: Find one confirmed email at a company, and you have cracked the pattern for everyone there.

section.p: If you can confirm — from a public source — that maria.velez@brightmail.com is real, you now know the recipe is first.last. So the boss you are looking for, Jason Karas, is a strong prediction: jason.karas@brightmail.com.
Where do you find that one confirmed address? Public places, all open:
• A company press release or a PDF report (try a search like "@brightmail.com" filetype:pdf).
• A staff "contact us" page.
• A public code repository, where developers' emails sit in the commit history.
• Domain-lookup tools that already catalogue a company's email format.

A small warning, so you look like a professional and not a spammer. Once you have your predicted address, do not email it to "test" it. Sending mail tells the person someone is poking around, which defeats the whole quiet purpose. There are ways to check if an address is real without sending anything, and tools built exactly for that — but for a beginner, the honest move is: find one confirmed address, apply the pattern, and treat the result as strong — not confirmed.

One more note. This pattern trick is cleanest for workplaces. For personal Gmail-style addresses, people mix in nicknames, birth years, and random numbers, so the guesses explode. Keep it for company domains, where discipline rules.
section.subtitle: Method 3 — Has this email been in a breach? (exposure only)
section.p: Big companies get hacked. It is sad but ordinary. When they do, lists of their users' emails — sometimes with passwords, dates of birth, or addresses attached — leak onto the internet. We call each event a breach.

For an investigator, breach exposure is a useful, careful signal. Note that word: exposure. We are checking whether an email showed up in a known leak, and which leaks. We are not going hunting for the stolen passwords, and we are certainly not using them.

The gold-standard free tool here is Have I Been Pwned (often written HIBP). You type an email, and it gives a simple list: this address appeared in the LinkedIn breach of such-a-year, the Dropbox breach of another, and so on. It does not show you the passwords. It shows presence — the fact of exposure, and the names and dates of the leaks.
Why is that useful to an OSINT investigator? Two reasons, both clean:

• It confirms the person had an account somewhere. If the email shows up in the "MyFitnessPal" breach, then this person used MyFitnessPal — one more site on your footprint map, sometimes for a service that has since shut down.
• It hints at timing. The breach has a date, which tells you the account existed by then. It sketches a rough timeline of the person's online life.

The line applies here too. Checking exposure — "yes, in these breaches" — is public knowledge about a public event, so it is safe. Reading, or using, the leaked passwords behind it is the door you already know you never open.

Breach data is also messy. Leaks get mislabelled. Old data gets recycled and re-sold under new names. So treat any breach hit as a lead, not a fact. It points you somewhere. It does not prove anything on its own.

And here is the part beginners get wrong, so learn it once and carry it everywhere: a zero result does not mean the address is safe, or fake, or unused. It means the tool has not indexed a leak that holds it — nothing more. Plenty of real, heavily-used addresses come back empty: their breaches were never added, or the address is newer than the leaks. "Zero breaches" reads as not found here, never as clean — the absence of a positive, not the presence of a negative. Treat it as a small nudge, never as a verdict.
What these checks actually look like on the screen — one hit, one empty:
section.subtitle: What a breach checker returns

cite.p: A breach check tells you where and roughly when someone had accounts. It never gives you permission to open one.

section.subtitle: Method 4 — The Gravatar pivot
section.p: One lesser-known trick feels like magic the first time it works.

There is a service called Gravatar — short for "globally recognized avatar." An avatar is just the little profile picture next to your name. Lots of websites (comment sections, developer sites, blogs) use Gravatar so that one photo follows you everywhere. You set it once, and it shows up across all of them.

And here is the quirk we can use: Gravatar links your photo — and sometimes a whole little profile — to your email. So if you have someone's email, you can sometimes pull back their photo, chosen username, real name, location, and links to their other accounts. From nothing but an email string.

You do not need to understand the math to use it. In simple terms: you take the lowercased email, run it through a standard fingerprint (called a hash — a fixed-length code made from the text), and ask Gravatar's public address for the matching picture and profile. Many tools do this step for you, so you just paste the email and read the result.

What you get, when it works: a face to put to the name, a username to feed into your other searches, and sometimes a location. Not everyone has a Gravatar, and many set only a photo. But when it hits, it hits big — a photo and a username from a single email is a wonderful thread to pull.
section.subtitle: Method 5 — Pivoting: email to username to name and back
section.p: Everything above shares one shape. You start with one piece of information, and it hands you another, which hands you another. This is called pivoting — swinging from one fact to the next, like crossing a river stone by stone.
The three stones you will hop between most often are email, username, and name. Here is how they feed each other:
• Email → username. The breach check or the Gravatar profile hands you a username the person likes to use, say jkaras_dev.
• Username → name. You search that username across social sites and forums (there are whole tools for this, covered in another chapter) and find a profile that shows a real name: Jason Karas.
• Name → email. Now you apply the company pattern trick from Method 2 and predict jason.karas@brightmail.com — and confirm it exists with the gentle "forgot password" check from Method 1.

See the circle? Each fact tightens the picture around the next. This is the real heartbeat of OSINT. No single search "solves" a person — you build them up, one confirmed stone at a time, checking each new fact against another source before you trust it.
section.subtitle: A worked case: one email opens a picture
section.p: Watch the whole thing as one small, made-up story. Every name and address here is invented — follow the moves, not the details.
You are handed a single email address: t.orsini@northvale-labs.com. That is all. Your job is to work out who this is.

• Step 1 — Read the address itself. Before any tool, just look. The domain is northvale-labs.com, a company. The local part is t.orsini, which smells like a f.last pattern — first initial t, last name orsini. So you are looking for someone named T-something Orsini at Northvale Labs — a weak read for now, but a free one, and you got it just by looking.

• Step 2 — Map the footprint. You run the email through a gentle "forgot password" check across common sites, using the method from earlier. A code-hosting site says "we've sent a reset link" — a clean yes, exists. But the professional network gives you the same polite message no matter what you type: "if an account exists, we'll email a link." That is deliberate. Many big sites now hide the differential exactly so people can't do what you're doing. So you do not get to conclude "she's on this network." You mark it unknown, not yes — no over-reading a message the site engineered to tell you nothing.

• Step 3 — Check the exposure. You look the email up on Have I Been Pwned. It appears in one breach, from a design-tools service, dated a few years back (the PixelForge Design, 2019 line in the box above). That confirms an old account elsewhere and roughly dates their online life. You write it down as a lead — nothing more. You do not go looking for any password. Out of habit you also check the company's generic info@northvale-labs.com — and it comes back zero breaches, zero pastes. You note it as a non-result, not a clean bill — again: a blank is not "clean."
• Step 4 — Try the Gravatar pivot. You feed the email to a Gravatar lookup. A profile comes back: a photo, a username torsini, and a listed city. Now you have a face and a handle from one address.

• Step 5 — Pivot the username to a name. You put the email in quotes and search it: "t.orsini@northvale-labs.com". The first page is mostly noise — those grey "email lookup" and "find anyone" sites that scrape an address, wrap it in ads, and know nothing you don't. You skip every one; they are junk dressed as results. Below the noise sits one real hit: a conference attendee list (a public PDF) naming Teresa Orsini, Northvale Labs. Then you pivot the handle instead — torsini across social and forum sites — and a second profile confirms the same name and employer. Two independent sources, so now you believe it. That matches your Step 1 guess. The stones connect.

• Step 6 — Confirm the pattern. Just to be sure of the recipe, you find one other Northvale Labs address in a public PDF on their site: m.dubois@northvale-labs.com. Same f.last shape. So the company pattern is confirmed, and t.orsini@northvale-labs.com sits neatly inside it — your original email verified from a second direction.

• A snag that does not resolve. On that same page you also spotted orders@northvale-labs.com and orsini.family@example-mail.com. Neither belongs to one person. The first is a role mailbox — a shared inbox a whole team reads. The second is a household account, shared by a couple or a family. Run it through Gravatar and get back one photo — whose face is it? You cannot tell. It could be Teresa, a partner, or an adult child who set up the account years ago. The address maps to a household, not a human, and no amount of pivoting splits it back apart. So you write down what is honestly true and no more: shared address — could be the owner or a family member — cannot separate them from here. That is where this thread ends. Not a clean answer. A partial one, marked as partial.

From one string of text, you now have a name, a face, a city, an employer, a rough timeline, and two confirmed accounts — plus one channel marked unknown and two addresses you refused to pin on a single person. Every step public, every step gentle, never once touching an account. Some of your sharpest moves were the ones where you didn't conclude: the hidden differential, the empty breach, the shared mailbox.

cite.p: A negative or ambiguous result is real data. "Unknown" written down honestly beats "yes" guessed wrongly, every time.

section.subtitle: Exercise: check your own exposure
section.p: Do this on your own email — the one that belongs to you. This is the safest possible practice, because you are the subject and you have every right.
1. Open Have I Been Pwned in your browser.
2. Type your own email address and run the check.
3. Read the list of breaches it comes back with. For each one, notice two things: which service leaked, and what year.
4. Write a short timeline for yourself: "I had an account on X by year Y." Notice how much of your own online history this sketches out — from one address.

5. As a bonus, look at what kind of data each breach exposed (some list "passwords," some "dates of birth"). If any breach exposed a password you still use anywhere, go change it. You have just turned an OSINT lesson into real self-defence.
Sit with how much your single email revealed. That feeling — "wow, it's all connected to this one thing" — is exactly what you now understand about everyone else's email. Use it with care.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • An email address is the master key because it is stable and unique — one person keeps it for years, so it quietly links to everywhere they have signed up, their real name, their photo, and their online history.

• The core moves are gentle and public: map where an email is used with the "forgot password" reveal, work out a company's email pattern from one confirmed address, check breach exposure on a service like Have I Been Pwned, try the Gravatar photo pivot, and swing between email, username, and name.
• Never cross the line you set at the start: confirm an account exists and read what a site volunteers, then stop. Logging in, guessing, or using a leaked password is not OSINT — it is a crime.

• Facts feed each other: email, username, and name form a loop, and each new fact is only worth trusting once a second source confirms it. A role mailbox or a household address maps to a group, not a person — write down what is honestly true and no more. "Unknown," written down honestly, beats "yes" reached wrongly.

cite.p: Turn it around. Shut this pivot down on yourself: use a unique address (or an alias) per site, turn on two-factor, and don't reuse one email as your username everywhere. See Appendix D (Take it back).

section.subtitle: Chapter Seven
section.p: Your own phone number, for a second.

You have had it for years. Maybe you have had it for a decade. You gave it to your bank. You gave it to your doctor. You put it on a job application. You typed it into a food-delivery app at 2 a.m. You saved it in a hundred friends' phones under your name.

A phone number is one of the most personal and most stable clues a person leaves behind. People change their email. People delete old social accounts. But most people keep the same phone number for a very long time. That is why I call it the personal anchor. It holds a person in place.

This chapter is about how to read a phone number, and how to safely see what is publicly tied to it. We will move slowly, and every term gets explained the moment it appears. Stay calm and careful the whole way: a phone number is not just data. It belongs to a real person.
section.subtitle: What a phone number actually is
section.p: One confusing thing to clear up first.

There is no single official "reverse phone book" for the world. You cannot type a number into one magic website and get the owner's name, verified and true. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something, and often selling stolen data.

What we actually do is smaller and honest. We read the structure of the number. We check where it shows up in public. And we check which apps the number is registered on. Each of those is a small clue. We stack the clues. That is the whole game.

cite.p: A phone number is a lead, never a conclusion. One hit points somewhere. It does not prove anything by itself.

section.subtitle: Reading the number itself
section.p: Before you look anything up, you read the number. This part is completely safe. You are not touching any network. You are not pinging anyone. You are just looking at the digits like a mapmaker looks at coordinates.
First, put the number into a clean international form. Investigators call this E.164 — that is just the name of the standard format. It looks like this:
+ then the country code then the rest of the number, with no spaces or dashes.
A made-up United States number written cleanly is +1 202 555 0134. A made-up United Kingdom number is +44 20 7946 0958. The + means "international." The first digits after it tell you the country.

• Country code — the leading digits tell you the nation. +1 is the US and Canada. +44 is the UK. +380 is Ukraine. +49 is Germany. This is the single most useful thing you learn, because it tells you which country's rules apply to everything you do next.

• Area or region prefix — the next block often points to a city or region, especially for landlines (a landline is a fixed home or office phone, not a mobile). For mobile phones this block points to the carrier that first issued the number.

• Line type — many free tools will also guess whether it is a mobile, a landline, or a VoIP number. VoIP means "voice over internet" — a phone number that lives on the internet, like Google Voice or a free texting app. This matters a lot. A VoIP number is cheap and anonymous. It belongs to no fixed person or place. If a number that claims to be someone's personal mobile turns out to be VoIP, be extra careful.
There is one trap here I must warn you about right away.

The carrier a tool shows you is usually the original carrier — the company that first handed out the number. But people can keep their number and switch companies. This is called number portability. So the number may say "Carrier X" while the person actually moved to Carrier Y years ago. Never write down "this person uses Carrier X" from a static reading alone. It is a weak reading, not a fact. This is the one place in the book that owns portability — when it comes up again later, I will just point back here.

cite.p: Reading the number offline tells you country, region, and line type. It never tells you the current owner.

section.p: The tools for this part come and go, and their names will change after this book is printed — most wrap the same open-source engine that validates numbers. Do not memorise any tool. Remember the steps: clean it to +country code number, then read country, region, and line type.
section.subtitle: Seeing what the number is publicly tied to
section.p: Now we go looking. Safely.
section.subtitle: Search the number in quotes across the web
section.p: This is the simplest move, and it is often the fastest path from a bare number to a real name or a business. People post their number all over the open web — in classified ads, business listings, forum signatures, old CVs, marketplace posts.
Type the number into a search engine inside quotation marks. Quotes tell the engine "find this exact thing." So you search "555 0134".
Here is the important part. People write their number a dozen different ways. So you search it a few different ways too:
• With the country code: "+1 202 555 0134"
• In the local style: "(555) 0134"
• With dashes: "555-0134"
• With spaces or dots

One format will hit a page that the others miss. When you find a page that lists the number, it almost always lists something next to it — a name, an email, a shop, a username. That neighbour is your next step.
Try more than one search engine. Google is not the whole internet. Bing and Yandex index different regional pages. For numbers from Eastern Europe and the region around it, Yandex is often stronger.

The trap here: number reuse. Phone numbers get recycled. When a person drops a number, the carrier gives it to someone new later. So an old page might show the previous owner. And businesses often share one number across many staff. Never assume the page and the person are a perfect match. Look for a second source that agrees.
section.subtitle: Crowdsourced "who called me" name apps
section.p: You have probably seen apps that claim to tell you who is calling. Truecaller, GetContact, and similar apps are the well-known examples. Here is exactly how they work, because understanding this protects you from a big mistake.

These apps do not have a secret official directory. They show you how other people saved this number in their own phones. When many users let an app read their contact list, the app learns that lots of people saved +1 202 555 0134 as, say, "Mike Plumber." So when you look it up, it shows "Mike Plumber."

cite.p: These apps cut both ways. The moment you install one and let it read your contacts, you hand over everyone in your phone — and your own number becomes searchable to others.

section.p: Sometimes this is genuinely helpful. One app, GetContact, is interesting because it shows you several names that different people saved for the same number. You might see "Mike Plumber," "Mike Landlord," and "SPAM." That cluster of names is a little story. It tells you the person's roles and how others see them, not just a single label.
But now the warning, and this is the most important warning in the whole chapter.

cite.p: Crowdsourced caller-name apps can lie, and they lie constantly. A name in one of these apps is a rumour, not a fact.

section.p: Why can they lie? Because the names are typed by random strangers. Someone can save your number under a joke name. Someone can save it wrong. An old contact can be years out of date. The number may have changed owners. The app just repeats whatever people typed. Bellingcat, a respected investigative group, warns plainly that these names have "mixed accuracy" and depend on how the number appears in other people's phone books.
So treat every returned name as a separate small clue. A name means much more if it shows up independently in two different apps or sources. A single name from a single app proves nothing.

One more thing, for your own safety. Many of these apps quietly upload your contact list when you use them. If you look someone up, you may hand over all your friends' numbers, and you may become searchable yourself.
section.subtitle: The strongest beginner move: number to messenger to username
section.p: Now for the single most productive path in phone work — the move that turns a lonely number into a real trail.
The core idea, in plain words.

A phone number is often the key to a messenger account. Messenger apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, and Viber let you find people by their phone number — that is a normal, built-in feature so friends can find each other. When you check a number in one of these apps, you may see a profile: a photo, a display name, a short bio, and sometimes a username.
That username is the treasure.

Because once you have a username, you are back in territory you already know. In an earlier chapter we learned that people reuse the same username across many sites. So a username you pulled from a messenger becomes a search you can run everywhere else. The chain looks like this:

p.strong: number → messenger profile → username → the rest of that person's online life.

section.p: Of all the paths in this chapter, Telegram is often the richest, because it can show a real @username even when it hides the actual phone number. And an @username is exactly the kind of clue that pivots across the whole web.

A gentle but firm caution. Checking a number in a messenger usually means saving it as a contact, and saving a contact can notify the person — they may see a new contact appear, or you may pop up in their "contacts who joined" list. So, as Chapter 3 covered, do this from a clean research account, never your own. And remember privacy settings: if someone set their app to "nobody can find me by my number," the check simply comes up empty. That is normal.

cite.p: A number often unlocks a messenger username. A username unlocks everything you already know how to search.

section.subtitle: A worked case: from a number to a name
section.p: Here is one fictional example, start to finish, so you see the clues stack. Every name and number here is invented.
You are trying to identify who posted a suspicious "car for sale" ad. The only contact detail in the ad is a phone number: +1 202 555 0177.
• Step 1 — Read the number offline. You clean it to +1 202 555 0177. The +1 tells you it is a US or Canada number. A free offline parser gives you this:
section.subtitle: What an offline number parser returns
section.p: An offline parser returns only these four things — country, region, line type, original carrier — never a name. The region is only where the number was born, not where the person lives now. And the carrier caveat applies: it is the original issuer, so you do not write "uses Verizon" anywhere. Write down only what is safe: "country = US, mobile, region = origin not home, carrier = unreliable (portability)." Now you know which country's web and search engines to lean on.

• Step 2 — Search the number in quotes. You search "202-555-0177", then "+1 202 555 0177", then "(202) 555-0177" on more than one engine. The dashed version hits an old post on a hobby forum where a user signed off with that number and the handle desertdrew. Interesting. But it is one page, so it is only a weak lead. (Had the parser tagged this VoIP — a Google Voice or free-app number — it would place nobody anywhere: no home region, no real carrier. You would grade the whole location angle weak and not build on it. A dead signal is fine; pretending it is strong is not.)
• Step 3 — Check crowdsourced name apps, carefully. Here is where the first app tries to fool you. It returns one loud name:
section.subtitle: What a caller-name app shows
section.p: If you were sloppy, you would write "the seller is Mike, a plumber" and go home wrong. But stop. A single crowd name is weak on its own — a rumour typed by strangers, not a fact. "Mike Plumber" does not match the forum handle desertdrew at all. Most likely the number was recycled and "Mike Plumber" is the previous owner, still living in strangers' address books years after he dropped it — the classic wrong answer a naive reader accepts and stops on. So you keep "Mike" as a weak, probably-dead lead. Then you check a second app: it returns "Drew" and "Drew Marketplace." A third app also returns "Drew." Now two independent apps agree on "Drew," and it lines up with the forum handle desertdrew. Corroboration lifts "Drew" from weak to moderate — but only because you refused to trust the first single name.

• Step 4 — Check messengers. You save the number as a contact and open Telegram. It resolves to an account showing a photo, the display name "Drew," and the username @desertdrew. Careful here — the owner set that name and username themselves, so they are not an independent source. The same person controls both the number and the name; a self-chosen name only corroborates that this account uses the handle desertdrew, it cannot confirm who the person is. So this does not lift "Drew." It stays at moderate, held there by the two independent apps and the forum post — sources the owner did not write.

• Step 5 — Pivot the username. You take @desertdrew and search it across other platforms, exactly as we practised in the username chapter. It appears on a photo-sharing site and a review site, both under the same handle, both placing him in the Washington DC area from Step 1. These are independent — the owner did not control what a review site or someone else's page says — and their agreement is what finally lifts "Drew" to strong. You now have a coherent picture: one person, one handle, one region, reachable at one number.

Notice what you did not do. No call, no login trick, no stolen data. You read public structure, searched public pages, used a normal app feature, and pivoted a public handle — confirming each lead against an independent source before trusting it.
section.subtitle: One advanced trick, and why beginners should skip it
section.p: You may eventually read about a clever technique where an investigator starts a "forgot my password" flow on a website, sees a hint like "we sent a code to the number ending in 77," and stitches together many such hints from many sites to rebuild a full hidden number.
I am naming it so you recognise it. I am also telling you to leave it alone for now.

Poking at a live login or account-recovery system to squeeze out account information sits in a legal grey area. Depending on your country and your intent, it can cross computer-misuse laws and app rules. It can also send a security alert to the real owner. This is not beginner ground. As a foundation-level investigator, you get remarkably far with the safe steps above and never need to touch it. If your work ever genuinely requires it, that is a moment for training, written authorisation, and a careful legal check — not curiosity.

cite.p: If a technique makes you interact with someone's login or recovery system, treat it as sensitive and step back. Foundations first.

section.subtitle: Exercise: safely look up your own number
section.p: The safest number in the world to practise on is your own. You already know the truth about it, so you can grade what the tools tell you. That makes it the perfect teacher.
Do this:
• Write your number in E.164. Put it in the + country code number form, no spaces or dashes. Confirm you got the country code right.

• Read it offline. Use any free number-reader to check country, region, and line type. Does it match reality? If it lists a carrier, notice whether it is your current carrier or an old one — this is how you feel portability with your own eyes.

• Search it in quotes. Search your own number in a few different formats, in more than one search engine. Where does it show up? You may be surprised what is public. Anything you find, someone investigating you could find too.
• Check a caller-name app. Look yourself up in one crowdsourced app. What name comes back? Is it right, wrong, funny, or blank? Sit with how unreliable it is even for a number you know perfectly.
• Write two or three sentences on what was accurate, what was wrong, and what surprised you.
That reflection is the real lesson. Feeling the tools be wrong about you is the fastest way to learn to never trust them blindly about a stranger.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • A phone number is a personal, long-lasting anchor. You read its structure offline (country, region, line type), you search it in quotes in several formats across several engines, and you check which apps it is registered on — every hit is a lead to confirm, never a fact.
• Crowdsourced "who called me" name apps show how strangers saved a number, so they are easily wrong and easily faked. A name only counts when two independent sources agree.

• The strongest beginner move is number → messenger profile → username, because a username drops you back into cross-platform search you already know. Do it from a clean research account, and leave login-and-recovery tricks alone as a legal grey area.
section.subtitle: Turn it around
section.p: Everything in this chapter can be pointed at you. Turn off "find me by my number" in your social apps and messengers, delete any caller-name apps — they upload your contacts and make you searchable — and consider a separate number for signups. Appendix D (Take it back) walks through it.

section.subtitle: Chapter Eight
section.p: This is the last chapter of the book. So let us do the thing the whole book was for.

We are going to run one real investigation, start to finish. One clue in. One honest little report out. Everything you learned in the earlier chapters gets used here — the search skills, the username hunt, the email checks, the phone checks, the confidence ladder, the OPSEC habits, and the ethical line you do not cross.

I invented this whole case. Every name, username, email, and phone number below is made up for teaching. None of them are real people. But the method is exactly how a professional works. Follow along slowly. Do not rush to the answer. In this work, how you get there matters as much as where you land.

One thing before we start. Keep your notes open the entire time. A blank text file is fine. Write down what you searched, what you found, when you found it, and how you found it. If you cannot trace a conclusion back to a note, you cannot defend it later. So we take notes from the very first click.

And one habit that saves cases: capture the page the moment you see it. Web pages change and get deleted — often the interesting ones, often right after you find them. So when something matters, take a screenshot, copy the exact web address, and save the page to a public web archive so there is a frozen, dated copy you can point to later. A note that links to a live page is only as reliable as that page tomorrow. A note that links to an archived copy is evidence.

cite.p: A finding you cannot trace back to a note is not a finding. It is a guess.

section.subtitle: The Setup
section.p: Here is our clue. Just one.

A small online marketplace for handmade goods got a complaint. A seller there, using the shop name "pinewicketcrafts", took money for an order and vanished. No delivery. No replies. The buyer asks a simple, fair question: is there a real person behind this shop, and is this shop connected to other shops that might be doing the same thing?

That is our objective. Notice how narrow it is. We are not "researching a person." We have a clear, answerable question. That focus is the whole job. A loose question makes you wander forever. A tight question tells you when to stop.
Write the objective at the top of your notes, word for word:

cite.p: Objective: Is there a real, findable person behind the shop "pinewicketcrafts," and is that shop linked to any other seller accounts?

section.p: Everything we do now serves that sentence.
section.subtitle: The Investigation
section.p: • Step 1 — Set up clean, then look before touching. Before I search anything, I open my research browser, not my personal one, signed out of my own accounts. No logging in, no messaging, no "contact seller" — passive work, public pages only. Then I write my first note: date, time, objective, and the single seed I have — the shop name pinewicketcrafts.

• Step 2 — Start with the plainest search there is. I put the shop name into a search engine, in quotes, exactly: "pinewicketcrafts". Quotes force an exact match, so I do not get pages about pine trees and cricket. Two things come back. First, the marketplace shop page itself. Second, a tiny result from a crafts forum where someone posted with the same name. Both go into my notes with their full web addresses and the time I saw them. I do not trust either yet. Right now they are leads, nothing more.

• Step 3 — Read the shop page like a document, not a story. The shop page is thin, but thin pages still leak. In the "About" section the seller wrote one friendly line: "Made with care in the workshop by Jordan." A first name. Good, but weak — a first name alone points at millions of people. I also note the shop opened eight months ago and lists a general region, not an address. I write down every fact and, just as important, I write down what is missing: no full name, no phone, no email on the page. Negative results are real results. They show how far I looked.

• Step 4 — Pivot on the username. Here is the first real pivot. People reuse handles. The same name they picked on one site, they often picked on ten others, because it is easy to remember. So I take pinewicketcrafts and check it across many platforms. (In an earlier chapter you saw the free username-search tools that do this — they simply ask each site, "does this name exist here?") The result is not a tidy list. It never is. Some sites say "not found," one rate-limits me, one loads a blank page, and two time out — the tool flat-out warns me which ones it could not read:
section.subtitle: What a username enumerator printed
section.p: So I do not have "the accounts." I have three candidates and a blind spot — a rate-limited site, a blank page that could be anything, and two that timed out. Four sites I could not actually read. I write that blind spot down, because a gap I know about is safer than a clean-looking list I trust too much. Same name is a lead, not proof. That caution is the difference between an investigator and a rumour.

• Step 5 — Confirm each candidate, and throw one out. Now I open the three candidates and look, instead of counting names. Two line up fast: the woodworking-forum profile talks about birdhouses, the marketplace shop sells birdhouses, same photo style, overlapping dates. Good — that is two independent places agreeing. But the third, the photo account, is wrong. I almost took it — the handle matched exactly. Then I actually read it: it is a teenager posting gym selfies and sneaker pics, last active years ago, nothing about wood at all. Someone else grabbed the same word first. Same handle, different human. I strike it from my notes and write why: "photos.example/pinewicketcrafts — REJECTED, unrelated person, no craft content, matched on name only." That rejection is not wasted work. It is the work. On the confidence ladder, two independent matches that survive a real look beat three that I never checked. I now put it at the moderate rung — the marketplace shop and the woodworking profile are probably one person — and I keep the door open, because I am still missing those two unreachable sites.

• Step 6 — Pivot from a username to an email. On the hobby-woodworking profile, in a public post asking for advice, the person signed off with a contact address so buyers could reach them: jordan.pinewicket@example-mail.com. That is a gift, and it is public, so I am allowed to note it. A new identifier means a new door. I run the safe, standard email checks you learned earlier — not to break into anything, but to see what is publicly tied to it. I check whether the address shows up in known public breach lists (a legitimate "has this email been in a leak" service), and I do a plain quoted search for the address itself. Here is what the breach check hands back — and notice the second line, because I also ran the shop's generic contact address to compare:
section.subtitle: What a breach checker returned

p.code: note: "0" is not "clean" — may be unindexed

section.p: Two things to read carefully. The personal address has been around for years and turns up in old breaches — so it is a genuine, used mailbox, not a throwaway made yesterday. The shop address returns nothing at all — but, per Chapter 6, a blank is not clean. I note it and move on. The quoted search then turns up one more real thing: the personal email left a public review on a second marketplace shop years ago, a shop called "oakwicketgoods."

• Step 7 — Follow the new lead, carefully. "oakwicketgoods." Different word, same odd middle piece — wicket. That echo is interesting, but an echo is not evidence. I do not declare the shops connected because two names rhyme. I go and look. The second shop is closed now, but its old public page still lists the same region and the same birdhouse photos. Same email in the review. Same craft. Same style. That is now two shops tied together by an email address and matching content — real corroboration, not a hunch. I write it down plainly: two seller accounts linked by one public email and matching product photos; moderate — two independent ties so far, with nothing against them.

• Step 8 — Pivot toward a phone, and read it honestly. The old "oakwicketgoods" page had one more scrap: a public post from years back where the seller offered a phone number for local pickup — +1 202 555 0147. I run the passive phone checks from the earlier chapter. And the lookup is a good reminder that a number lies as often as it talks:
section.subtitle: What an offline number parser showed

p.code: line type: VoIP (not a home carrier)

section.p: Read that and cool down. A VoIP number is an app, not a doorstep — its "region" is where the number was born, not where its owner sleeps. So this does not place Jordan anywhere. It is a weak signal, and I grade it weak. What it is good for is one thing: a plain search of the number turns up the same digits on both shop pages — so it is a third independent thread between the two shops, on top of the email and the photos. That third thread is what lifts the shop-to-shop link from moderate to strong; the number itself still stays weak as a way to place a person, and that is all I let it do. Then the same search quietly surfaces something else — a personal social profile, in the name "Jordan Alvarez," with home-life photos, a partner tagged, and what looks like a house and street in the background. I note that surname, but I do not lean on it: it hangs off this one weak VoIP number and nothing else has confirmed it. A single weak lead does not earn a place in my conclusion — so "Alvarez" stays a flagged, uncorroborated maybe, and my finding stays with what I can stand behind: a seller who goes by Jordan. And here I stop.

• Step 9 — Stop at the line, on purpose. Notice what just happened. My question was about a seller and whether shops are linked. It was not about a person's home, their partner, or where they sleep at night. The trail could keep going — I could try to pin down the exact address, the partner tagged in that photo, the daily routine. I do not. Not because I could not, but because I should not. That material is outside my objective, it is intrusive, and chasing it would turn a fair inquiry into surveillance of a private life — a real person's, with a real family, who came into this only as the name behind a shop. So I write a note — an honest one: "Trail extended toward home address and family; stopped here. Out of scope and intrusive. Not collected." Knowing where to stop is not weakness. It is the whole reason people can trust this craft at all.

cite.p: The skill that makes you a professional is not how far you can go. It is knowing where to stop — and writing down that you stopped.

section.p: Step back now and look at what we actually built — and what we threw away. From one shop name, we reached a first name, two confirmed accounts (after binning a third that was a stranger with the same handle), a public email, a second linked shop, and a phone number that we graded weak but that still tied the two shops together. Likely one operator who goes by Jordan — with a surname that surfaced once and stays uncorroborated. Each step was a small, checkable pivot. Each finding was weighed on the confidence ladder before it earned the next step — and the rejected account and the "no records" blank are part of the trail, not embarrassments hidden from it. And we drew a clean line where the public interest ended and a private life began.

That is the loop from the very first chapter, run for real: exposure (public scraps left online) → pivot (turn each scrap into the next door) → attribution (carefully deciding it is one person) — all inside the rules.
section.subtitle: The Report
section.p: A finding nobody can read is a finding that does not count. So we write it up. Short, plain, and honest. A good beginner report answers four things: what I was asked, what I found, how sure I am, and what I did not do. Here is ours.

cite.p: Case: pinewicketcrafts non-delivery inquiry Date: (today's date) Objective: Determine whether a real, findable person is behind the shop "pinewicketcrafts," and whether it links to other seller accounts.

section.p: What I found. The shop "pinewicketcrafts" appears to be run by a real individual who goes by the first name Jordan. (A surname, "Alvarez," surfaced from a single weak phone lead; I flag it as unconfirmed and do not treat it as established.) The seller is linked — at the strong rung — to a second, now-closed marketplace shop, "oakwicketgoods," and, at the moderate rung, to a woodworking-hobby profile. The links rest on a shared public email address (jordan.pinewicket@example-mail.com), matching product photos, and reused contact details.

What I ruled out. A photo-sharing account with the identical handle "pinewicketcrafts" turned out to belong to a different, unrelated person (no craft content, matched on name only). I rejected it. Two sites were unreachable during my username check, so my picture is not complete, and I say so.

How sure I am, and why. The shop-to-shop link is strong; the tie to the woodworking profile is only moderate; and it is not confirmed — I want to be clear about that. The conclusion does not rest on any single clue; it rests on a few independent public sources agreeing — matching craft and photos and a reused email across two shops. The phone number I graded weak on purpose: it is a VoIP/app number, so it corroborates the shop link but places nobody anywhere. If the email turned out to be shared by two people, my confidence would drop, so I flag that as the point that would change the picture.

What I did not do, and what I could not confirm. I did not contact the seller or any account. I did not log in anywhere or interact — all collection was passive and from public pages. I stopped when the trail pointed toward a home address and family members, because that is outside this inquiry and intrusive. I could not confirm the seller's exact legal identity or intent; "vanished on an order" is what the buyer reports, and I found no independent proof of fraud — only that two accounts are linked and the operator is likely findable. That distinction matters: I am reporting connections I verified, not a crime I proved.
Sources. (A short numbered list of every page, with its web address and the time I viewed it — including the searches that found nothing, and the account I checked and rejected.)

Read that report again and notice its tone. It never oversells. It says how sure, not just what. It admits the gaps. It shows the line I refused to cross. A report like this is something you can hand to another person and they can check every step. That is the goal. Not to sound clever — to be checkable.

cite.p: Write findings, not verdicts. Say how sure you are, show your sources, and admit what you did not do.

section.subtitle: A second case: the one that doesn't close
section.p: I want to show you one more, and it is the most important in the book — because it fails. Real work does this far more often than the tidy story above, and a beginner who never sees it will think they did something wrong when it happens to them. They didn't. Sometimes the honest answer is "I can't say," and reaching that answer cleanly is a professional skill, not a failure.

The request: a buyer left a glowing review on a marketplace that reads like a fake, signed only "Rae M." — is it a real customer or the seller praising their own shop? One name fragment, nothing else.

I work it the same disciplined way. A search for the handle raem turns up two live accounts that both fit. One is a Rae Molina, active in the same craft scene, in roughly the right region — plausible. The other is a Rae Mercer, who has interacted with this exact seller before — also plausible. Two real people. Both could be "Rae M." I try to break the tie. The email pivot dead-ends: no public address for either. The photo pivot dead-ends: neither profile has a usable image. A quoted search for "Rae M." plus the shop name gives me nothing new. I have two candidates, each sitting at the weak rung, and nothing that lifts one above the other.
So I stop — and I write the honest ending:

cite.p: Finding: Could not attribute. Two plausible individuals ("Rae Molina," "Rae Mercer") fit the fragment "Rae M."; no public evidence separates them. Confidence: weak, split across two candidates. I cannot say whether the review is genuine or self-written. Recommend not acting on this until a stronger identifier appears.

section.p: Read that. It names the dead end plainly. It refuses to pick the more convenient answer just to hand someone a name. That refusal is the finding. An investigator who forces a confident answer out of weak evidence is not more useful than one who says "I can't say" — they are more dangerous, because someone might act on the guess.

cite.p: "I could not confirm this" is a finding too. Write it whenever it is true.

section.p: One more note before you go — who the subject is changes the rules. Both cases above were consumer scenarios: a scam seller, a suspect review. If instead you are ever doing this to vet a job candidate or check an employee, stop and remember the sidebar from Chapter 2: the extra laws (FCRA, anti-discrimination rules, biometric consent) switch on. In that world the discipline grows one more rule — you stop and do not record things that are none of the job's business (someone's religion, health, pregnancy) exactly the way we stopped at Jordan's home address here. And for formal hiring decisions, that work often has to run through a licensed screener, not a hobbyist. Different subject, extra rules. Know which world you are in before you start.
section.subtitle: Where to Keep Learning
section.p: You have finished the foundations. Now the only way forward is reps. Here is how to get them safely and for free.

Practise on yourself first. You are the one subject you are always allowed to investigate fully. Search your own name, your own old usernames, your own email in a breach checker. It is eye-opening — and a little uncomfortable — to see your own footprint the way a stranger would. Bonus: everything you find, you can then go clean up. Best OPSEC lesson there is.

Do OSINT challenges and CTFs. "CTF" means capture the flag — a game where you solve puzzles to find a hidden answer. There are OSINT-flavoured ones where you geolocate a photo, or trace a fake persona across sites. They are safe (the "targets" are invented for the game), they are graded, and they build the exact pivot muscles from this chapter. Search for beginner OSINT CTFs and quizzes; many are free and browser-based.

Try a supervised missing-persons event — carefully. Groups like Trace Labs run "search parties" where volunteers use OSINT to help find real missing people, working strictly inside the law and a firm no-contact rule. This is real, meaningful work, but it is not a beginner free-for-all: you follow their OPSEC guide, you use a research account, and you never interact with anyone. Go in humble, read their participant guide first, and learn from people who have done it for years.

Read the reputable guides, not random blogs. A few sources are trusted across the whole field — for example, Bellingcat's online investigation toolkit and their beginner verification guides. These are written by people who do this for a living and are careful about the law and the ethics. Bookmark the good ones. Come back to them.

Keep the habits, not just the tools. Tools will change. New sites appear, old ones die, apps get renamed every year. The process does not. Tight question, take notes from action one, pivot with discipline, weigh every finding on the confidence ladder, stop at the ethical line, write it up honestly. Learn that, and any new tool is just a new door for the same method.
section.subtitle: A Bridge to Volume Two
section.p: This book was the foundations: the loop, the rules, precise search, usernames, email, phone, the confidence ladder, and the basics of staying safe and staying ethical.

Volume 2 goes deeper. We will get serious about OPSEC — real research accounts, isolated environments, and controlling what you leak while you look. We will move into images and places: reverse image search done properly, and geolocation — figuring out where a photo was taken from what is in the frame. We will build timelines and relationship maps, and learn the structured ways professionals fight their own bias so their conclusions hold up. Everything there stands on what you just practised here.

For now, you have done the thing this book was for. You ran an investigation, from one small clue to an honest report, and — the part that matters most — you knew where to stop. That is the whole craft in miniature. There is a person at the end of every trail you will ever follow. Keep your notes. Stay curious. Stay kind. And I will see you in Volume 2.
— Yehor
section.subtitle: Exercise
section.p: Run your own tiny case, on yourself, using only the steps in this chapter.

• Pick your seed. Choose one old username you used years ago. Write it at the top of a fresh notes file, with today's date and this objective: "Find what public accounts and info still trace back to this old username of mine."
• Search it exactly. Put the username in quotes in a search engine. Note every result with its web address and the time you looked.
• Pivot it across platforms. Use a free username-checker to see where that name still exists. Note each hit as a lead, not proof.
• Confirm or reject. For each hit, decide: is this really me, or someone who picked the same name? Write your reasoning and a confidence level for each.
• Find your own line. At some point you may find something private — an old address, a family member. Practise stopping. Write the note: "Reached private info; stopped; out of scope."
• Write the four-part report. What you were asked, what you found, how sure you are, and what you did not do. Keep it under one page.
Then do the useful part: clean up whatever you found. That is your first real investigation and your first real OPSEC win.
section.subtitle: Recap
section.p: • One clue is enough to start — a single public scrap, worked with a tight question and disciplined pivots, can carry you all the way to an answer.

• The mess is the job, not a mistake — real trails have wrong hits, dead ends, blank results, and tools that time out. A run with no rejected leads is not a clean run; it is a careless one. Write down what you threw out and why.

• Weigh before you walk — every finding gets a rung on the ladder (weak → moderate → strong → confirmed), and you never build the next step on an unconfirmed lead; only several independent sources agreeing earns confirmed.

• The report and the line are the craft — a professional writes findings honestly (how sure, what sources, what they did not do) and knows exactly where the public interest ends and a private life begins.

epigraph.p: What you can do now — and what comes next.

section.p: Look back at where you started this book.

A username was just a username. An email was just an address. A phone number was just digits. Now you know the truth: each of them is a thread, and you know how to pull it — gently, in order, confirming as you go.

You learned the one loop the whole craft runs on — exposure → pivot → attribution. You learned the rules that keep you a professional instead of a problem. You learned to protect yourself before you look at anyone else. You learned to search like someone who knows what they're doing, and to turn a username, an email, or a phone number into the beginning of a real, honest picture.
That is the foundation. Everything ahead is built on it.
section.subtitle: The honest part
section.p: You will be tempted, now that you can see, to see everything. Resist it. The skill you have started to build is quiet power, and quiet power is judged entirely by how you use it. There is a real person at the end of every thread — someone who never agreed to be looked at. Look only when you have a good reason. Confirm before you conclude. And when the trail leads somewhere you have no business going — stop. That instinct, more than any technique in this book, is what makes someone trustworthy with this work.
section.subtitle: Where you go from here
section.p: The next thing to do is simple: practice. Run the loop on yourself. Run it on things you own. When you're ready for real, guided practice, the OSINT community runs open challenges and events — safe, legal places to sharpen everything you just learned. (You'll find a starting list in the appendix.)

Then, when the single clues start to feel easy, you're ready for Volume 2 — Cross-Platform Attribution, where one thread becomes many, and you learn to follow a person across every place they exist at once.
You came in able to search. You're leaving able to investigate.

epigraph.p: A glossary, the method on one page, and where to practise.

section.subtitle: A — Plain-words glossary
section.p: • OSINT — finding things out using only public, open information.
• Exposure — a trace someone left in the open (a username, photo, number, post).
• Pivot — using one clue to find the next one.
• Attribution — being confident that the clues point to one real identity.
• Sock puppet — a clean, separate account used for research, never your real one.
• OPSEC — protecting yourself while you work, so your looking leaves no trace.
• Dork — a precise search using operators (like quotes or site:) to force better results.
• Metadata — the hidden data inside a file (for example, when and sometimes where a photo was taken).

• Confidence ladder — how sure you are, in four fixed words used all through this book: weak (one unconfirmed clue), moderate (two independent clues agree), strong (three or more agree, nothing contradicts), confirmed (independently nailed down and checkable).
section.subtitle: B — The method on one page
section.p: 1. Start from one clue. Write down exactly what you have.
2. Ask a small question. "What can this one thing give me?"
3. Pivot. Turn each answer into the next question.
4. Climb the confidence ladder. Never conclude on one clue — confirm with two or three independent ones.
5. Write it down as you go. Save what you found and where you found it — screenshot it and save a copy to a web archive before the page can change.
6. Know when to stop. No good reason, or crossing a line? Stop. And if the evidence never gets past weak, "could not confirm" is a real, honest answer.

cite.p: Exposure → pivot → attribution. Confirm before you conclude.

section.subtitle: C — Where to practise (safely and legally)
section.p: • Investigate yourself first. It's the one target you're always allowed to fully explore.
• OSINT challenges and CTFs. The community runs open, legal puzzle events built exactly for learning these skills.
• Missing-persons search events (such as those run by Trace Labs) let you practise for a genuinely good cause, alongside experienced people.
• Public investigation guides from respected teams (for example, Bellingcat's toolkit and exercises) give you real problems to solve.
Start small, stay legal, and keep the method in front of you. Skill comes from reps, not from tools.

A note on the tools in the exercises. They come in two shapes. Some are ordinary websites — you just open them in a browser and type. Others (many username checkers and email tools) are small free programs you install, and some of those run in a terminal — a text window where you type commands — rather than with buttons. Neither is better; they just have different on-ramps. If a tool wants a terminal and that is new to you, do not let it stop you: start with a browser-based equivalent, learn the method, and pick up the terminal ones later. And you never need to spend a cent to practise anything in this book.
section.subtitle: D — Take it back: shrinking your own footprint
section.p: Once you have investigated yourself, you have a map of your own exposure. Now use it. Every technique in this book runs on scraps you left in the open — so the defence is simple: leave fewer scraps, and take back the ones you can. Work down this list in order; the first items give you the most protection for the least effort.

• Change the passwords that leaked. Run your emails through a breach checker (Chapter 6). For every address that shows up in a breach, change that password and every other place you reused it. This is the single highest-value thing on the page.
• Turn on two-factor everywhere that matters. Email first, then anything with money or messages. An app-based code beats a texted code. A leaked password alone stops being enough to get in.
• Break the username thread. You saw in Chapter 5 how one reused handle links all your accounts. For anything you want kept separate, use a different name. Retire old handles you no longer use.
• Close and delete dead accounts. The forum you used once in 2016 is still leaking. If you will not use it again, delete it — do not just abandon it. Fewer doors, fewer pivots.

• Turn off "find me by my number / email." On social apps and messengers, switch off the settings that let a stranger find your profile from your phone number or email. This kills the phone-pivot from Chapter 7.

• Uninstall contact-name apps and revoke contact access. Those caller-ID apps uploaded your whole address book — and made your number searchable to others. Remove them, and revoke contacts permission from apps that do not need it.
• Strip location and metadata before you post. Photos can carry the place they were taken. Turn off location tags in your camera, and check the privacy settings that geotag your posts.
• Lock down what strangers can see. Set old posts and photo albums to friends-only. Review the "public" side of each profile as if you were a stranger looking in — because someone will be.

• Use the removal routes that exist. Search your name; where a data-broker or "people-finder" site lists you, most have an opt-out or removal form. It is tedious, but it works. Re-check every few months — some relist you.
• Recheck yourself on a schedule. Exposure grows back. Run the self-investigation from Chapter 8 twice a year and clean up whatever is new.

When the person looking already knows you. This whole book leans on one comfort — that a stranger has to guess whether two accounts are the same person, and guesses can be wrong. That comfort disappears when the searcher is someone who already knows your old usernames, your number, your email, your face, and your family's names — an ex, a stalker, a harasser. For them, the "same name isn't the same person" protection does not apply; they have the ground truth. If that is your situation, understand two hard things. First, a real photo you already posted, or a relative who tagged you, can sometimes not be fully un-leaked — the honest fix may be changing the username, number, or email itself, not just hiding it. Second, this is bigger than a checklist. Reach specialist help: a domestic-violence hotline, an address-confidentiality program, or local police — people who do exactly this for a living.

Protecting your family. Every pivot in this book works on your kids and partner too. Lock down minors' accounts hard: private by default, no location tags, no findable-by-number or -email, and talk with them about what a stranger can rebuild from an oversharing post. Do the self-investigation on your family's public footprint, gently, and clean up together.

cite.p: The best protection is the same skill as the best investigation: know exactly what you are leaving in the open — then decide, on purpose, what stays.

section.subtitle: E — Templates you can copy
section.p: Steal these. Paste them into a note file and fill the blanks. They turn the habits in this book into something you actually run.
The four-part report. Every finding you hand to anyone fits this skeleton:

p.code: OBJECTIVE: (the single question, in one sentence)
+ the independent sources it rests on)
WHAT I RULED OUT: (leads checked and rejected, and why)
WHAT I DID NOT DO: (limits, the line I stopped at,
archived copy — include the dead ends)

section.p: The running note (one row per step). Keep this open from the first click:
The confidence-ladder cheat card. Never write a conclusion without a rung — and here is exactly what earns each one:
• weak — one clue, unconfirmed (a matching name, a single crowd label, a VoIP number). A lead, never a conclusion.
• moderate — two independent sources agree (e.g. content + dates, or two separate apps). "Independent" means they could not have simply copied each other.
• strong — three or more independent sources agree and nothing contradicts them.
• confirmed — independently nailed down, and another person could re-check every step and reach the same answer.

cite.p: If you cannot name the rung, you have not finished the finding.
